lead: One path through everything for this call. Each topic: learn it, check yourself with multiple choice (say 'I don't know' when you don't, tick 'I'm guessing' when you are), explain the open question aloud, then compare and rate yourself. The squares show where you stand; test a module or everything, weakest first.

onepage.lead: The points to know before the call, from your banking copilot handbook and the research. Skim it; anything that doesn't click in one read, open its topic. Say only what you can explain one level down: they will dig into any term you use, and 'I don't know, but here is how I'd find out' is a good answer.

points.d: Use models where language ambiguity is the hard part, deterministic systems where correctness is: a deterministic financial core with a probabilistic language interface.
The model interprets, retrieves, summarises and proposes. It is never the source of truth for money, positions, identity, permissions, policy or execution state.
Insight is read-only and cites; recommendation is simulation with no action; action needs policy, auth, explicit confirmation and idempotent execution.
Normalise (code), route by intent and entities (model and code), retrieve (code), plan or answer (model), policy and tool call (code), execute and verify (code), respond grounded.
Intent is what they want; an entity is what you need to do it. Resolve entities to real ids through APIs, never from a nickname.
A conversation API for the user and a bounded tool API for the model; each tool declares a side-effect class: read-only, reversible, or consequential.
Write the action with an idempotency key before calling the provider; on a timeout, check status before retrying. 'Probably sent' is not a financial state.
A cheap calibrated classifier for the high-volume intents, an LLM for low-confidence or compound turns. Calibration means 0.92 is right about 92% of the time.
BM25 for exact terms, dense for paraphrase, fuse and rerank, then access and effective date in code. A matched retired policy is still wrong.
Compact dialogue state with real ids plus a short window; never cache balances or execution status without a freshness contract.
TF-IDF is hard to beat on narrow tasks; static, contextual and sentence embeddings each have a job; embeddings are an index, not a ledger.
BPE merges frequent pairs, WordPiece merges by likelihood gain, SentencePiece trains BPE or unigram tokenizers on raw text.
Routing F1 and the confusion matrix, entity resolution, Recall@K, grounded claims, task success and cost, duplicate actions. Review by volume times cost times severity.
Put it next to confirmed resolution, repeat contact and abandonment; containment rises when people give up.
The square root of d_k keeps softmax out of saturation; heads learn different subspaces; attention is quadratic, the KV cache linear; FlashAttention moves less memory with the same maths.

modules.title: The map of NLP and conversational AI
modules.blurb: Place any term they use on one map: the stages of an assistant turn, the eras of the stack, and the NLP underneath.

topics.title: One turn through the stack
topics.brief: A conversational assistant is a stack of stages, not one model: text or speech comes in, understanding turns it into an intent and entities, dialogue management decides the next step against the state, the backend does the work, and a reply goes out. The nuance people miss: errors compound down the chain, so a 95% accurate ASR feeding a 98% accurate NLU gets about 93% of turns through both, and each stage needs its own metric.
points: Input: text from chat or SMS, or audio that ASR turns into text; for voice, endpointing decides when the user has finished
Understanding (NLU): the intent is text classification, entities and slots are sequence labelling, and out-of-scope is the option to answer 'none of these'
Dialogue management: holds the state (what has been collected, where the user is in the task) and picks the next action: ask, confirm, call the backend, hand off
Backend and tools: the APIs that look up a balance or move money; the only stage that changes anything in the world
Response generation: templates or approved copy in classic bots, an LLM phrasing the result in newer ones; TTS speaks it for voice
Around the stack: safety checks, logging and evaluation at every stage, and a path to a human
production: Classic platforms (Dialogflow CX, Lex, CLU, Rasa, Kore.ai, Cognigy) build this as classification plus labelling plus a state machine
LLM-first stacks fold understanding and generation into one model, but keep classifiers and embeddings in front as routers and guards
A small classifier answers in milliseconds on a CPU, against about a second for an LLM call, so it takes the confident turns and sends only uncertain or open-ended ones to the LLM
Voice adds ASR at the front and TTS at the back, and the user talking again can interrupt any stage

read.label: Hugging Face: LLM course, ch. 1, NLP and large language models
read.why: What NLP covers and where LLMs changed it, in one page

mcq.q: A voice bot's ASR is 95% accurate and its NLU is 98% accurate. Roughly what share of turns get through both stages correctly?
o: About 98%, because the NLU sets the ceiling
About 95%, because the weaker stage sets the ceiling
About 93%, because the errors compound down the chain
About 96.5%, the average of the two stages
Above 98%, because the NLU repairs most ASR errors
mcq.why: 0.95 times 0.98 is about 0.93 if the errors are independent. In practice it is often worse, because an NLU trained on clean typed text does badly on transcripts with recognition errors.

mcq.q: A user says 'move 500 dollars to savings'. Which stage should own the decision that a confirmation is needed before the transfer runs?
o: The dialogue manager, applying a rule for money movement
The NLU model, since it extracted the amount
The response generator, when it phrases the reply
The backend API, after the transfer has posted
The ASR, based on its transcription confidence
mcq.why: Deciding the next action is the dialogue manager's job, and a money rule belongs in code there. Low ASR or NLU confidence can raise the need to confirm, but they feed the decision rather than own it.

mcq.q: Which pairing of assistant stage and NLP task is right?
o: Intent is sequence labelling; entities are text classification
Intent is retrieval; entities are text generation
Intent is generation; entities are retrieval
Intent is text classification; entities are sequence labelling
Intent is language modelling; entities are parsing
mcq.why: An intent is one label for the whole message, a classification. Entities are spans inside it, so each token gets a label: sequence labelling, the same family as NER.

open.q: Walk me through what happens in one turn when a customer types 'what's my balance on the Roth' to a bank assistant.
open.probe: Whether you see the assistant as a stack with a job per stage, or as one model that does everything
a: Text comes in and is normalized; for voice, ASR and endpointing come first
NLU returns the intent (check balance) and an entity (account type: Roth IRA), with confidence
Dialogue management checks the state: is the user authenticated, does 'the Roth' resolve to one of their accounts, is anything missing
The backend balance API returns the figure from the system of record; the model never produces the number
The reply is a template or an LLM phrasing the number it was given, logged for evaluation; if any stage is unsure, it clarifies or hands off

say: I think of it as a stack, not one model. Something understands the message, something holds the state and decides the next step, and the backend does the work.
At alfred_ the model reads the message and picks a typed tool, but the things in play live outside the model as entities with ids, so 'that meeting' resolves to a real record.
The model can propose. Code decides what actually runs.
avoid: Saying alfred_ has a trained intent classifier: intent and slots come from an LLM with typed tool schemas, validated in code

topics.title: Understanding: intent, entities, out-of-scope
topics.brief: NLU turns one message into a structured guess: which task the user wants (the intent), the values it needs (entities, which fill slots), and whether it is something the assistant handles at all. The nuance: out-of-scope is a first-class answer. Without it, a classifier forces every message into the nearest intent, and the confident wrong answer is worse than asking again.
points: Intent: a label for what the user wants done, chosen from a fixed set; a text classification problem
Entities: the values inside the message (an amount, a date, an account type), found by prebuilt extractors, lists with synonyms, regexes or a learned tagger
Slots: the entities a task needs; the ones collected so far are part of the dialogue state
Out-of-scope: a 'none of these' outcome, from a trained negative intent or a confidence threshold
Confidence: the score that decides act, confirm or fall back; useful only if it is calibrated, so a 0.9 is right about 90% of the time
production: The platforms name the out-of-scope part: CLU's None intent, Dialogflow CX's default negative intent and no-match event, Lex's AMAZON.FallbackIntent
Entities mix extractors: prebuilt dates and numbers, lists with synonyms for closed sets, regex plus validation for IDs
LLM-first stacks get intent and slots from function calling: each tool is an intent and its typed arguments are slots
Microsoft CLU reports per-intent precision, recall and F1 with a confusion matrix, because overall accuracy hides weak intents

read.label: Microsoft Learn: CLU evaluation metrics
read.why: Per-intent precision, recall and F1, and the confusion matrix, on a real platform

mcq.q: A flight bot is told 'I want to buy a book' and confidently returns BookFlight. What is its NLU missing?
o: A better entity extractor for product names
An out-of-scope outcome, a negative intent or a threshold
More training phrases for the BookFlight intent
A larger language model behind the classifier
A dialogue state tracker for the whole session
mcq.why: A classifier with no 'none of these' option must pick some intent. Near misses like 'buy a book' are exactly what a negative intent or a threshold is for.

mcq.q: 'Transfer 200 to my savings tomorrow.' Which split into intent and entities is right?
o: Intent: savings; entities: transfer, 200, tomorrow
Intents: transfer and schedule; no entities needed
Intent: tomorrow; entities: the amount and the account
One intent per account type, here transfer_to_savings
Intent: transfer; entities: amount, destination account, date
mcq.why: The action is the intent and the information it needs is entities. One intent per account type multiplies near-duplicate intents that collide.

mcq.q: Why must a confidence score be calibrated before you set act, confirm and fall-back thresholds on it?
o: So the scores across all intents add up to exactly one
So the model trains faster on the next data refresh
So the top intent always scores above 0.5
So a 0.9 score is right about 90% of the time
So one threshold works for every future model version
mcq.why: A threshold is a bet on what a score means. An overconfident model can be wrong at 0.99, which makes any cutoff meaningless. Softmax scores summing to one says nothing about calibration.

open.q: A customer writes 'my card got eaten by the ATM, send a new one to my old address'. What does your NLU return, and what is hard about it?
open.probe: Intent against entities, multi-part messages, and knowing when not to guess
a: The main intent is replace card, with the card as an entity that has to resolve to one of their cards
'My old address' is an entity that needs resolving against records, and it hides a second request: an address change
Classic NLU returns one intent per turn, so the second request is split out, queued, or handled by a planner
An address change is high risk, so it needs authentication and an explicit confirmation before anything ships
If the scores are close or the reference is ambiguous, ask one short question instead of guessing

say: I'd say the intent is the task and the entities are the values it needs, and I'd always keep a 'none of these' answer.
Honestly, at alfred_ we don't have a trained intent classifier or an NER model. Intent and slots come from an LLM picking typed tools, and code validates the arguments.
Entity resolution for contacts and events is deterministic code with thresholds. Same parts, different machinery.
avoid: Calling softmax scores 'probabilities you can trust' without calibration

topics.title: Dialogue state, the backend and the reply
topics.brief: Dialogue management is the part that remembers and decides: it holds the state (slots collected, where the user is, whether they are authenticated) and chooses the next action. The backend executes and the reply reports. The nuance: state must live in code with real ids, not only in the transcript, because the transcript is what a model can misread.
points: Dialogue state: the structured record at each turn: active task, slots filled, pending action, authentication status
Policy: the rule for the next step: ask for a missing slot, confirm, call the backend, clarify or hand off
Classic form: a state machine, such as Dialogflow CX pages, Lex slot elicitation or Rasa flows
Backend and tools: typed APIs with server-side validation; the model may propose a call, code authorises it
Response generation: approved copy for anything regulated, an LLM for phrasing; figures come from the backend, never from the model
production: Dialogflow CX: flows are topics and pages are states, each with a form of required parameters and routes out
Rasa CALM: an LLM turns the message into commands such as start flow or set slot, and deterministic flows run the steps
Wells Fargo's Fargo, as reported: the LLM extracts intent and entities, while the APIs for transfers and lookups never pass through it
A balance or order status is fetched and then phrased; the model is never the source of the number

mcq.q: Halfway through a transfer the user says 'actually make it 500'. Where should the new amount go so later steps use it?
o: Only in the transcript, which the model rereads each turn
In the NLU training data for the transfer intent
Into the slot in the dialogue state, then reconfirmed
Into the response template for the confirmation
Straight to the backend, sending the transfer at once
mcq.why: The slot store is the authoritative state, so a correction updates the slot and triggers a fresh confirmation. Leaving it only in the transcript means a later step may read the old value.

mcq.q: Why do teams keep templates or approved copy for some replies even with an LLM in the stack?
o: Templates always read more naturally than generated text
LLMs cannot produce text in a fixed format
Templates remove the need to track dialogue state
Approved copy makes the NLU more accurate
Regulated statements and figures must match what was approved or fetched
mcq.why: A disclosure or a balance has to be exactly right, not plausibly worded. Generation is fine for phrasing around content the system already owns.

open.q: In an LLM-based assistant, where does dialogue state live, and why not let the model keep it in the conversation?
open.probe: Whether you know the transcript is context, not authoritative state
a: State is a structured record: active task, slots, pending action, auth status, the ids of the things in play
Keep it in code and give the model a compact slice of it plus a short transcript window
Long transcripts get misread or truncated, and the same message can behave differently in a fresh session and a long one
References like 'the second email' resolve to ids held in state, and the backend reads the state, not prose
The trade-off is more engineering, but the state becomes testable and replayable

say: The way I'd do it, the state lives in code and the model gets a compact view of it.

At alfred_ I built entity management in chat: the things in play, an email, an event, a contact, are typed entities with ids and lifetimes outside the model. So 'that meeting' resolves to a real record instead of a guess.
The transcript is context. The state is the truth.
avoid: Saying the model 'remembers' the account or the order: say where the id is held

topics.title: Classic NLU, LLM-first and the hybrid
topics.brief: Classic platforms are a trained intent classifier, entity extractors and an authored state machine: predictable, cheap and auditable, but every new task costs training data and authoring. LLM-first stacks fold understanding and generation into one model: flexible, few labels, slower and harder to certify. Most banks run a hybrid, and the real question is where the line sits: the model interprets, code owns the action.
points: Classic: classification plus labelling plus a state machine; per-intent metrics and easy audits
LLM-first: one model reads the message, picks a tool and writes the reply; handles long-tail phrasing and several requests in one message
Hybrid: a fast classifier or small model takes confident turns, an LLM takes uncertain or open-ended ones, deterministic flows own transactions
Why classifiers survive: milliseconds on a CPU against about a second per LLM call, and a stable label for routing, analytics and compliance
What changed: building the intent list stopped being the bottleneck, and evaluation became it
production: Bank of America's Erica, as reported: still 700 plus curated intents rather than an LLM, for a closed set of high-volume actions
Amazon (EMNLP 2024 industry track): sending a turn to the LLM only when a SetFit classifier was uncertain stayed within 2% of the LLM's accuracy with 50% less latency
Rasa CALM and Copilot Studio moved intent matching to an LLM that reads flow or topic descriptions, while flows still own the steps
Dialogflow CX keeps flows for authentication and payment, and adds generative playbooks and generative fallback for open conversation

mcq.q: A bank has 40 stable, high-volume intents, plenty of labelled logs, and a voice channel with tight latency. What is the strongest default for intent routing?
o: A large LLM on every turn, with no classifier
A fine-tuned encoder classifier, with an LLM for the uncertain tail
Keyword rules only, since the intent set is small
An LLM that writes new intents as traffic arrives
Nearest-neighbour search over the training phrases alone
mcq.why: Stable labels, lots of data and tight latency favour a fine-tuned encoder. The LLM earns its cost on the uncertain or open-ended turns the classifier is unsure about.

mcq.q: What does an LLM-first design give up compared with a classic intent stack?
o: The ability to handle paraphrases
Support for multi-turn conversations
Any way to call backend APIs
Predictability and per-intent auditability
The ability to answer 'none of these'
mcq.why: The LLM handles paraphrase and multi-turn well. What it loses is a fixed label per turn that you can measure, audit and explain to a model risk team, and repeatable behaviour across runs.

mcq.q: In the hybrid most banks run, which job does the LLM typically not do?
o: Execute the money movement itself
Interpret long-tail phrasing
Extract slots from a messy message
Answer FAQs from retrieved content
Take turns the classifier is unsure about
mcq.why: The LLM interprets and phrases. Execution goes through deterministic flows with validation and confirmation, so the model never does the transfer itself.

open.q: Explain to a product manager the difference between a classic NLU bot and an LLM agent, and why a bank might still want the classic parts.
open.probe: A balanced trade-off, not 'LLMs replaced intents'
a: Classic: a classifier picks the intent, extractors fill slots, and authored flows run the task
LLM agent: one model understands, picks tools and writes replies, with far less training data per task
Classic strengths: predictable, cheap, fast, measurable per intent, easy for model risk review
LLM strengths: long-tail phrasing, several requests in one message, open questions
So a hybrid: a router in front, flows own money movement, the LLM handles open questions grounded in approved content; Erica staying intent-based for closed actions is the example

say: I don't think it's classic or LLM. It's where you draw the line.

At alfred_ we have a lean first pass: a fast model answers simple turns from what it can read, or escalates to a heavier agent. Code guards turn a reply that promises an action or claims it's done into an escalation instead of shipping it.
Same idea as a bank's hybrid. A fast path in front, and code owns what actually happens.
avoid: Implying hands-on time on a classic platform: say you've read how each one models the problem

topics.title: Where classification, embeddings and LLMs sit
topics.brief: Underneath the assistant is the NLP field: text becomes units (tokens), units become numbers (from sparse counts to dense embeddings), and tasks run on top (classification, labelling, retrieval, generation). Each era replaced hand-built features with learned representations. The nuance: the older rungs did not die, and TF-IDF, small classifiers and embeddings still sit in front of LLMs as routers, retrievers and guards.
points: Tokenization: text into words, subwords or bytes; LLM cost and quirks with numbers and other languages start here

Sparse to dense: bag of words and TF-IDF count words; static embeddings (word2vec, GloVe) give one vector per word, so 'bank' has one meaning; contextual ones (BERT) give one per occurrence; sentence embeddings give one per text
Text classification: intent, sentiment, topic; from logistic regression on TF-IDF, to fine-tuned encoders, to zero-shot LLMs
Embeddings in the assistant: semantic search over FAQs and RAG, clustering logs to find new intents, nearest-neighbour routing
LLMs: very large decoders pretrained on next-token prediction, then instruction and preference tuned; in the assistant they understand, plan tool calls and phrase replies
Eras: rules, statistical models on hand-built features, neural seq2seq with attention, the Transformer (2017), BERT (2018) making pretrain then fine-tune the standard, then LLMs
production: TF-IDF is still the default sparse baseline, strong for topic-like classification and lexical matching
Sentence embeddings drive semantic search, clustering and the retrieval half of RAG in front of the LLM
Encoders (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa) for understanding, decoders (GPT, Llama) for generation, encoder-decoders (T5, BART) for input-to-output tasks
Machine translation is the task that produced seq2seq, attention and the Transformer

read.why: ELMo to BERT, GPT and T5; read to the end of BERT

read.label: Hugging Face: LLM course, how do Transformers work
read.why: The history and the three shapes: encoder, decoder, encoder-decoder

read.label: Stanford: Speech and Language Processing (SLP3), table of contents
read.why: The chapter list is itself a map of the field

mcq.q: Why does a static embedding such as word2vec struggle with 'bank' in 'river bank' and 'bank account'?
o: It cannot represent words seen fewer than ten times
It splits 'bank' into subwords that lose the meaning
It gives one vector per word, whatever the sentence
It weights 'bank' down because the word is common
It encodes word order but not word meaning
mcq.why: Static embeddings learn one vector per word type, so both senses share it. A contextual model like BERT computes a vector per occurrence from the whole sentence.

mcq.q: Which job in a conversational assistant is a sentence embedding model best suited to?
o: Executing a transfer once the slots are filled
Generating the reply text in the right tone
Measuring word error rate on call audio
Deciding whether an action needs confirmation
Finding the FAQ article closest in meaning to a question
mcq.why: Sentence embeddings place texts with similar meaning close together, which is what semantic search and RAG retrieval need. Execution, confirmation and phrasing belong to other stages.

mcq.q: What thread runs through NLP's eras, from n-gram models to LLMs?
o: Models got smaller and cheaper at each step
Hand-built features were replaced by learned representations
Rules were removed from every production system
Each era moved from generation toward classification
Labelled data mattered more at each step
mcq.why: Statistical models needed hand-built features; neural models and then pretrained Transformers learned the representations. Rules still survive for narrow high-precision cases, and LLMs need less labelled data, not more.

open.q: Give me the map of NLP in two minutes, and put conversational AI on it.
open.probe: Breadth with structure, and whether you can place real systems and your own work on it
a: Foundations: normalization and tokenization, morphology, tagging and parsing
Representations: sparse (bag of words, TF-IDF, n-grams) to dense (static, contextual, sentence embeddings)
Tasks: classification, sequence labelling, QA, summarization, translation, retrieval, dialogue, extraction
Eras: rules, statistical, neural, Transformers, LLMs; the thread is learned representations replacing hand-built features
Conversational AI is a stack over the map: intent is classification, entities are labelling, FAQ is retrieval, the reply and tool calls are generation

say: I'd draw it as a tree: how text becomes units, how units become numbers, the tasks on top, the eras, and how you measure it.
The thread is that learned representations replaced hand-built features. Conversational AI isn't a branch, it's a stack that uses several tasks in one turn.
In MetaRAG I used TF-IDF weighted embeddings, which is the old rung and the new one working together.
avoid: Calling BERT a generative model: it is an encoder, used for understanding

topics.title: One metric per stage
topics.brief: Each stage of the stack has its own metric, and each metric hides something. Accuracy hides rare intents when classes are imbalanced, word error rate hides the digits and names that matter, and perplexity says how well a model predicts text, not whether it answers correctly. The end-to-end number is task completion; the per-stage numbers tell you where to look.
points: ASR: word error rate, but slot-level accuracy on digits, names and amounts is what breaks tasks
Precision and recall: of what I flagged, how much was right; of what was there, how much I found; F1 drops if either is low
Intent: macro-F1 with per-intent recall and a confusion matrix; with 95% of data in one class, always predicting it scores 95% accuracy and near-zero macro-F1
Dialogue state: joint goal accuracy, the share of turns with every slot right
Generation: BLEU and ROUGE are cheap overlap, weakly tied to quality; open-ended replies need rubric judges calibrated against people
End to end: task completion, with escalation and repeat contact as guardrails
production: Microsoft CLU reports per-intent precision, recall and F1 with a confusion matrix
MT-bench: strong LLM judges agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, about the human-to-human rate, but showed position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases
Perplexity is exp of the average negative log-likelihood: a language model measure, not an answer-quality one

read.why: Per-intent P, R and F1, and how the confusion matrix is read

read.label: arXiv: Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-bench
read.why: The abstract and the bias section: when a model judge can be trusted

read.label: Stanford: SLP3, ch. 4 Logistic regression and text classification
read.why: Skim to the evaluation section: precision, recall, F1, micro and macro

mcq.q: 150 intents, ten of which carry most of the traffic. Which headline metric shows rare intents failing?
o: Micro-F1, because it pools every decision
Overall accuracy on the test set
Perplexity of the intent model
Macro-F1, because every intent counts equally
BLEU against the reference labels
mcq.why: Micro pools all decisions, so the ten big intents dominate it. Macro averages per-intent F1, so a rare intent failing pulls it down. Report both, lead with macro, and show per-intent recall.

mcq.q: After retraining, micro-F1 rose from 0.91 to 0.93 while macro-F1 fell from 0.80 to 0.72. What most likely happened?
o: It got better on every intent equally
The test set shrank, so both scores are noise
It improved on rare intents and slipped on big ones
The labels changed, so the numbers can't be compared
It improved on big intents and got worse on rare ones
mcq.why: Micro follows the high-volume intents and macro weights every intent equally. Micro up with macro down means the big ones improved while several small ones got worse.

mcq.q: Why is perplexity a poor way to judge a banking assistant's answers?
o: It measures how well text is predicted, not whether answers are right
It can only be computed for encoder models
It rewards short answers over long ones
It needs a human reference answer for every turn
It ignores the tokens at the start of a reply
mcq.why: Perplexity is about predicting held-out text. A fluent, likely answer can still be wrong, ungrounded or unhelpful, so task metrics and judges are needed.

open.q: Your intent model reports 94% accuracy and the business says the bot feels broken. What do you look at?
open.probe: Whether you know what accuracy hides and can go from a metric to a cause
a: Check the class balance: if a few intents carry the traffic, accuracy is mostly about them
Look at macro-F1, per-intent recall and the hot cells of the confusion matrix
Compare the clean test set with real traffic, sliced by channel, since voice transcripts carry ASR errors
Measure end-to-end task completion and escalation: a right intent with a wrong slot still fails
Read a sample of failed conversations to find the cause the numbers point at

say: I'd first ask what the 94% is over. If a few intents carry the traffic, accuracy hides the rare ones, so I'd look at macro-F1, per-intent recall and the confusion matrix.
Then task completion end to end, because a right intent with a wrong slot still fails.
And I'd read real failed conversations. At alfred_ we built a replay bench over real production turns, graded by a person, because the aggregate never told us why.
avoid: Quoting BLEU or ROUGE as the measure of a chatbot's quality

modules.title: Conversation design
modules.blurb: Design a task end to end in the room: failure paths, confirmation, repair, handoff, voice, and where determinism lives.

topics.title: Designing a new use case
topics.brief: Start from the tasks people actually bring, ranked by volume and by the cost of getting them wrong, then write the happy path as a sample dialog and read it aloud. The nuance: the failure paths are written before anything is built, because nearly every bad assistant has a good happy path and nothing else. Success is task completion, not fewer turns.
points: Scope: top tasks from call and chat logs, ranked by volume and risk, not from the product catalogue
Sample dialogs: written and read aloud; a prompt that reads fine often sounds wrong spoken
Failure paths first: no-match, no-input, system error, correction, digression, out of scope, handoff
Cooperative principle (Grice): say enough and no more, be relevant and clear; one question per turn, ending with what the user should do next
Slots: ask in the order people know the information, and accept over-answering
Persona: a style guide and constraint set (4 to 6 traits, how it says it is automated, what it never discusses), never a pretence of being human
production: Google's persona recipe: brainstorm adjectives, narrow to 4 to 6 traits, pick an archetype, write a one-paragraph description
Dialogflow CX prefills form parameters from the matched intent, and Rasa collect steps can skip a question already answered, so over-answering costs no extra turn
Rasa's conversation-driven development is the same loop after launch: review real conversations, tag them, fix in batches
In finance the persona never offers personalised investment recommendations; FINRA Notice 24-09 says existing communications, recordkeeping and supervision rules apply to AI-generated communications
Klarna's CEO later said cost-driven automation had lowered quality: measure resolution on hard cases, not only containment

mcq.q: You are scoping version one of a bank assistant. Where should its list of tasks come from?
o: The product catalogue, one intent per product
Call and chat logs, ranked by volume and cost of error
A workshop where designers imagine common requests
The FAQ page, one intent per question
The platform's prebuilt starter templates
mcq.why: Real logs show what people ask and how they say it. Ranking by cost of error as well as volume puts the risky tasks, like disputes, in scope early.

mcq.q: Why is turn count a poor primary metric for a conversation design?
o: Turn count cannot be measured on voice channels
More turns always mean the user is more engaged
Fewer turns can mean the user gave up or was handed off early
Turn count depends mostly on ASR quality, not design
Turn count only changes when intents are added
mcq.why: Task completion is what the design is for. Turn count and abandonment are guardrails around it, because a short conversation can be a failed one.

mcq.q: In an enterprise bank assistant, what is the persona mainly for?
o: A style guide and constraint set for every prompt and line of copy
Making users believe they are talking to a person
Choosing which LLM the assistant runs on
Deciding the shape of the intent taxonomy
Setting confidence thresholds per channel
mcq.why: The persona keeps tone consistent and sets limits, including how the bot says it is automated and what it must never say. It is not meant to pass as human.

open.q: Design the conversation for checking an order's status by voice. Where do you start, and what do you write before you build?
open.probe: Task-first design with the failure paths written up front, not a happy-path script
a: Start from the top tasks by volume; write the happy path as a sample dialog and say it aloud
Write the failure paths: no-match, no-input, the order service timing out, a change of mind, a request for a human
Slots in the order users know them; the order number is alphanumeric, so offer spelling or keypad and confirm it before the lookup
No explicit confirmation for the status itself, since a read changes nothing (a cancellation would); decide handoff triggers and payload now
The metric is task completion, with escalation and repeat contact as guardrails, not turn count

say: I'd start from what people actually ask for, ranked by volume and by how bad a mistake is, from logs if there are any.
Then I write sample dialogs and read them out loud. Before I build anything I write the failure paths: silence, not understood, the backend failing, a change of mind, wanting a person.
Pretty much every bad bot I've seen had a good happy path and nothing else.
avoid: Leading with the persona's personality before the tasks and failure paths

topics.title: No-match, no-input and the error ladder
topics.brief: Three kinds of error need three treatments: no-input (silence), no-match (heard but not understood) and system error (understood, but the backend failed). Help escalates with each miss, and there is always a way out. The nuance: never repeat a failed prompt word for word, and count failures per conversation, not only per state, or a user can bounce between states and never reach the exit.
points: No-input: silence, a first-class event on voice; rephrase and offer options, never 'I didn't hear you'
No-match: heard, not understood; a short rephrase with one brief apology, then options or an example
System error: say so plainly, and do not make the user repeat what they already gave
The ladder: rephrase, then options or examples, then a way out (a person, a menu, another channel) after about two failures
Tone: messages specific to the state, no blaming, no over-apologising; a global 'Sorry, I didn't get that' is what people quote when they complain
production: Dialogflow CX: numbered event handlers, sys.no-match-1 to 6 and sys.no-input-1 to 6, set at flow, page or parameter level, plus reprompt handlers for form filling
Alexa's ladder: first repeat, then explain, then suggest leaving the task
AWS guidance for Lex and Connect: a short first prompt, a more detailed retry, then DTMF-only fallback
Review no-match rate per page every week, and how many sessions recover after the first reprompt: it points at design or NLU gaps

mcq.q: The NLU understood the request, then the account service timed out. Which error type is this?
o: No-input: the user went silent
No-match: the input was not understood
System error: understood, but the backend failed
Out of scope: the bot does not support it
Disambiguation: two intents scored close
mcq.why: No-match is about understanding; a system error happens after understanding succeeded. The fix is to say so and keep what the user gave, not to reprompt as if they were unclear.

mcq.q: After a first no-match, what should the assistant do next?
o: Repeat the same prompt word for word, more slowly
Rephrase briefly, and on a second miss add options or an example
Transfer to a human straight away
Say 'Sorry, I didn't get that' and wait
Ask the user to spell out the whole request
mcq.why: If the words failed once they will likely fail again. A rephrase, then options, gives the user a new way in; a verbatim repeat only adds a turn and frustration.

mcq.q: Why also count consecutive failures across the conversation, not only per state?
o: Platforms only store counters at conversation level
Per-state counters make the NLU retrain more often
Conversation counters make the bot apologise less
It halves the number of handlers to write
A user bouncing between states would otherwise never reach the exit
mcq.why: Per-state counters reset when the user moves. Someone who keeps failing in different states can loop for ever unless the total is counted.

open.q: A caller goes silent after 'What's your account number?', then mumbles something the bot can't parse. Walk me through what the bot does, turn by turn.
open.probe: Escalating help, messages specific to the state, and a guaranteed exit
a: First silence: they are probably looking for it, so a patient reprompt with a hint ('you can say it or type it on the keypad')
Then the no-match: a short rephrase with one brief apology, giving the format expected
Second miss: switch mode to keypad entry with an end character, rather than looping on recognition
After about two failures in total: a person or another path, carrying what was already collected
Afterwards: measure recovery after the first reprompt and no-match by page, and fix the prompt or the NLU it points at

say: I count errors and escalate the help. The first miss gets a short rephrase, not the same prompt again. The second adds options or an example.
After about two, I offer a way out, a person or a menu. And every message is specific to where the user is.
I'd review no-match by page every week, because it points straight at design gaps and NLU gaps.
avoid: Saying 'I didn't hear you' on no-input, or using one global sorry message

topics.title: Confirmation in proportion to risk
topics.brief: Confirm in proportion to the cost of being wrong times the chance of being wrong. Implicit confirmation ('Okay, a table for two') is the default: it keeps the flow and lets the user correct. Explicit yes-or-no is for actions that are costly or cannot be undone. The nuance: low recognition confidence raises the bar even for cheap values, and over-confirming is a real cost too.
points: Implicit: restate what was understood and move on; the user can correct it
Explicit: a yes-or-no before payments, deletions, sending on someone's behalf, names and addresses
Confidence raises it: a misheard name on a voice call gets read back even when the action is cheap
Who decides: code, by the type of action, not the model's opinion of it
After execution: for a transaction, confirm again with a reference number
Over-confirming: costs turns and trust; watch turn count and drop-off
production: Lex returns a transcription confidence and up to three alternative transcriptions; its docs suggest reprompting on low confidence and checking close candidates (John against Juan) against a database
Cognigy builds in the middle band: above the confidence threshold (default 0.4) accept, between it and the reconfirmation threshold (default 0.2) ask 'did you mean X?', below it nothing is found
A transfer reads back amount, source, destination and date, and needs a clear yes before it executes

read.why: Implicit by default, explicit for costly actions

read.label: AWS: Lex V2 transcription confidence

mcq.q: 'Okay, checking the balance on your savings account.' What kind of confirmation is that, and when is it right?
o: Implicit; right when a mistake is cheap and easy to correct
Explicit; right before any irreversible action
Implicit; right before payments and deletions
Explicit; right whenever ASR confidence is high
Neither; it is a disambiguation prompt
mcq.why: It restates the understanding and moves on, so the user can correct it. That fits a read-only lookup; money movement needs an explicit yes.

mcq.q: Which action most clearly needs an explicit yes-or-no confirmation?
o: Reading out a fund's expense ratio
Showing the last five transactions
Checking an order's delivery status
Sending a wire to a new payee
Switching the conversation to Spanish
mcq.why: A wire to a new payee is costly and hard to reverse. The others are reads or easy to undo, so implicit confirmation keeps the flow.

mcq.q: A caller says a name and ASR returns 'John' and 'Juan' with close scores. What is the best next step?
o: Pick the higher score and continue
Check both against the database, then ask a closed question or have them spell it
Transfer to a human immediately
Ask the caller to repeat the whole request
Store both names and decide at the end
mcq.why: The N-best list is information. If only one exists in the records, use it with a read-back; if both exist, a short closed question or spelling settles it before acting.

open.q: A customer asks the assistant to move money between two of their accounts. Design the confirmation.
open.probe: Confirmation proportional to risk, enforced by code rather than left to the model
a: Implicit confirmation on each slot as it is collected, so mistakes surface early
Low confidence on any slot triggers a read-back of that slot, digits in groups
Before execution, an explicit read-back of amount, source, destination and date, and a clear yes
A correction updates one slot and triggers a fresh explicit confirmation; after execution, a reference number
Code enforces the explicit step so no prompt can skip it; watch drop-off so it does not over-confirm

say: I think the rule is cost of being wrong times chance of being wrong. Implicit by default, explicit before anything you can't undo.

At alfred_ I built the confirm flow: side-effecting tools first return a preview, and only a second call with an explicit confirmation executes. There are floors no prompt can override: destructive actions and external sends always confirm, and a bare 'yes' can't approve several sends.
Idempotency keys make the retries safe.
avoid: Describing alfred_'s confirmation as scoring or verdicts: it is a preview, then an explicit confirm, with code floors

topics.title: Repair: corrections, digressions, disambiguation
topics.brief: Real conversations leave the happy path: the user changes a value, asks a side question, switches task, or says something that fits two intents. Repair is how the assistant handles those turns and gets back to the task without losing state. The nuance: each kind needs a different mechanism, and none of them shows up in per-utterance accuracy, so each is tested as its own scenario.
points: Correction: spot that an earlier slot is being updated, change it, re-run only what depends on it, and reconfirm (explicitly when money is involved)
Digression: answer the side question, then return to the paused task
Topic switch: the task is abandoned; with money half-specified, ask 'do you want to cancel the transfer?'
Disambiguation: when the top two intents are close, one short closed question ('the card or the account?'); 0.75 against 0.72 is close, 0.95 against 0.65 is not
Over-answering: fill every slot the user gave and skip those questions
Authoritative state: the account, order id and authentication status live in the slot store, not in chat history
production: Dialogflow CX: route groups at flow or agent level let 'cancel', 'agent' or FAQ intents match anywhere; intent routes take priority, which handles digressions and also causes accidental exits from half-filled forms
Rasa ships repair as patterns: correction, clarification, cannot handle, continue interrupted, cancel flow, skip question, chitchat, human handoff, repeat, user silence

Copilot Studio's planner reuses recent history to fill inputs, but the history is limited, and Microsoft's docs said its Multiple Topics Matched disambiguation was not yet called under generative orchestration
Conversation-level regression tests: scripted multi-turn transcripts, as Rasa and Dialogflow CX both recommend

mcq.q: Mid-transfer, the user asks 'what's the daily limit, by the way?' and then wants to carry on. What is this turn, and what should happen?
o: A correction; update the amount slot and reconfirm
A digression; answer it, then return to the transfer
A topic switch; cancel the transfer and start over
Out of scope; decline and repeat the last prompt
A no-match; rephrase the amount question
mcq.why: A side question with the task still wanted is a digression: answer, keep the transfer's slots, and resume. Nothing already given has changed.

mcq.q: Mid-transfer, the user says 'no wait, from checking, not savings'. What should the assistant do?
o: Restart the transfer from the first question
Answer it as a side question and keep the old value
Update the source slot, re-run what depends on it, and reconfirm
Hand off, because the user seems confused
Ignore it until the final confirmation step
mcq.why: This is a correction: one slot changes. Dependent checks such as the balance on the new source re-run, and the changed transfer gets a fresh confirmation.

mcq.q: The top two intents score 0.74 and 0.71. What should the assistant do?
o: Take the top intent, since it scored higher
Fall back to the no-match handler
Hand off to a human at once
Run both flows and keep whichever finishes
Ask one short either-or question between the two
mcq.why: A small margin means the model cannot tell them apart. One closed question costs a turn; guessing wrong in a banking flow costs more.

open.q: A user is halfway through a transfer, says 'actually make it 500', asks about fees, then says 'ok go'. Walk me through what the assistant should do.
open.probe: Whether repair is designed state handling or left to luck
a: 'Make it 500' is a correction: update the amount slot, re-run the balance and limit checks, and mark the transfer as needing confirmation again
The fees question is a digression: answer from approved content while the transfer stays paused with its slots
'Ok go' must not approve it: the amount changed, so read back the full transfer and get an explicit yes
The slot store is the truth, not the chat history, so the 500 is what executes
Test exactly this sequence as a scripted multi-turn scenario, since per-utterance accuracy never catches it

say: I treat corrections and digressions as designed paths, not errors. 'Actually make it 500' updates one slot and gets a fresh confirmation, never a silent edit.
A side question gets answered and then we go back to where they were. The things that must survive, the account, the amount, whether they're authenticated, live in state, not in the chat history.
I'd test each of these as its own scenario, because that's where happy-path bots break.
avoid: Saying 'the LLM handles context' as the whole answer: name where the state lives and how it is tested

topics.title: Handoff to a human
topics.brief: A handoff is a feature, not a failure: the right case reaches a person fast with the context attached, so the customer never repeats themselves. The triggers are designed up front. The nuance: optimising containment alone pushes toward trapping people, and regulators have named the bot that cannot hand off.
points: Triggers: an explicit request (transfer at once, no more attempts), a second failure, low confidence on a high-stakes intent, frustration, topics marked human-only
Human-only in finance: complaints, disputes, hardship, bereavement, suspected fraud, anything that sounds like personalised advice; routed on detection, not after the bot has tried
Payload: a short summary, the intent, identifiers and authentication status, slots collected, what was already tried; not a 40-turn transcript
Warm against cold: in a warm transfer the agent is briefed before the customer joins; escalation is cold unless someone designs it otherwise
No agents available: a callback or a ticket, never a dead end
Frustration: behaviour (repeated reprompts, barge-in on every prompt, pressing 0) beats a sentiment score on short utterances; let the model signal raise priority, not decide alone
production: Dialogflow CX has a live agent handoff signal with custom metadata; contact centre platforms such as Twilio Flex pass the transcript and context to the agent's desktop
Agent assist points the same stack at the human: knowledge suggestions, suggested replies, live and after-call summaries (Google Agent Assist lists these)
The CFPB's 2023 chatbot spotlight describes 'doom loops' with no route to a person, which makes the escalation path a compliance control
Measure handoff quality: repeat contact within 7 days, how often the agent re-asks identification, transfer-to-resolution time, satisfaction split by bot-only and handed-off
Escalated transcripts and agent corrections are the best labelled data: mine them weekly for missing intents and broken flows

mcq.q: On the first turn the customer types 'agent'. What should the assistant do?
o: Try to resolve it once more, then transfer
Ask why they want a person before deciding
Offer a menu of self-service options first
Transfer at once, passing what it already knows
Wait for a second request to be sure
mcq.why: An explicit request is honoured immediately. Making people argue with the bot is the doom loop regulators have called out.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between a warm and a cold transfer?
o: In a warm transfer the agent is briefed with context before the customer joins
A warm transfer always goes to a senior agent
A cold transfer happens outside business hours
In a warm transfer the bot stays listening on the call
A cold transfer drops the call and calls back later
mcq.why: Warm means the context arrives first: summary, intent, identifiers. Cold means the customer lands in a queue and often explains again.

mcq.q: Why is containment rate a risky primary goal for a bank assistant?
o: It cannot be measured on voice channels
It drops whenever new intents are added
It ignores how quickly the NLU responds
It only counts authenticated sessions
It rewards keeping customers in the bot when a person would resolve it
mcq.why: Containment counts conversations the bot finished, not problems solved. Pushing it alone traps people; pair it with resolution, repeat contact and satisfaction on handed-off cases.

open.q: When should our assistant hand off to a human, and what should the agent receive?
open.probe: Designed triggers and payload, and handoff treated as a feature rather than a failure
a: Triggers: an explicit request at once, a second failure, low confidence on a high-stakes intent, frustration signals
Human-only topics in finance (disputes, fraud, hardship, complaints) route on detection, before the bot tries
Payload: a short summary, the intent, identifiers and auth status, slots collected, what was tried; warm transfer when stakes or emotion are high
No agents free: a callback or a ticket, never a dead end
Measure repeat explanation, re-asked identification and resolution after handoff; read escalations weekly for fixes

say: I wouldn't treat every escalation as a failure. An explicit request transfers at once, and so does a second failure, a high-stakes topic or clear frustration.
What matters is what travels with the customer: a short summary, the intent, identifiers, what was already tried. I'd measure how often people have to explain again after the transfer.
And I'd read a sample of escalations every week. They're the best data we have.
avoid: Treating containment as the goal, or a handoff as a failure

topics.title: Voice is not chat with a microphone
topics.brief: A listener cannot scan, so voice prompts are short with the question last, lists hold three options or fewer, and silence and barge-in are designed events. Recognition errors dominate voice failures, and identifiers are the worst case: there is no language prior for a random account number, so one wrong character fails the lookup. The nuance: overall word error rate can look fine while exact identifier match is poor, so measure accuracy on the words that carry meaning.
points: Prompts: short, context first and the question last, three options or fewer, no tables
Silence and barge-in: a first silence usually means the user is searching, so reprompt with a hint; barge-in on for short prompts, off for disclosures that must be heard in full
Identifiers: letters and digits sound alike (P and B, M and N, O and zero); read back in groups, and use check digits or the caller's own accounts to correct or reject
DTMF: keypad entry as the deterministic fallback after one failed retry; tones avoid transcription errors and keep spoken digits out of the transcript
Chained errors: ASR and NLU errors multiply, so test the NLU on real ASR output, pass the N-best list, and keep thresholds and test sets per channel
Chat: buttons and longer answers, scroll-back, but fragments, typos, pasted text, and no timeout signal
production: A Speechmatics write-up (vendor-reported) notes 96.6% word accuracy can still mean only 77% exact identifier match

Lex lets each slot take audio, DTMF or both, with timeouts, an end character, and wait-and-continue while the caller finds a number; the AWS pattern is a short prompt, a detailed retry, then DTMF only
Endpointing: published tuning guidance puts about 250 ms of silence for purposeful IVR callers and about 400 ms where people think aloud, with a sentence-completeness signal on top

One published budget for a cascaded pipeline: about 80 ms endpointing, 120 ms ASR, 180 ms LLM and 70 ms TTS for under 500 ms perceived; for slow tool calls, a short real acknowledgement, never fake filler
Vanguard's own materials mention a voice bot for address changes among 70 plus bots: a narrow transactional voice task with identity checks

mcq.q: Why put the question at the end of a voice prompt?
o: The listener cannot scan back, so the last thing heard is what they answer
ASR is more accurate on the last words of a prompt
Barge-in only works after the prompt finishes
TTS engines stress the final sentence of a prompt
It makes the prompt quicker to synthesise
mcq.why: Voice is linear and has no scroll-back. Context first, the question last, and the whole prompt short, so the user answers what was asked.

mcq.q: A voice bot's word accuracy is above 96%, yet account lookups often fail. What is the most likely reason?
o: The TTS voice is too fast for older callers
Identifiers are all-or-nothing, and one wrong character fails the match
Word accuracy above 95% means the NLU must be at fault
The endpointing is set too slow for the callers
The bot uses implicit confirmation for names
mcq.why: Word accuracy averages over easy words. An account number has no language prior and every character must be right, so exact-match accuracy can be far lower.

mcq.q: Why not reuse the chat channel's test utterances to test the voice channel?
o: Voice needs ten times as many test cases as chat
Chat utterances are too long for voice prompts
Typed text lacks the recognition errors and spoken phrasing of real audio
Voice test sets must be recorded by the design team
Chat utterances contain emojis the ASR cannot read
mcq.why: Real voice input is a transcript with ASR errors and different phrasing. Testing on typed text overstates voice accuracy; build the voice set from real call audio.

open.q: We're adding a voice channel to our chat assistant. What changes?
open.probe: Channel sense: prompts, recognition errors, identifiers, fallbacks and measurement
a: Prompts: short, question last, three options or fewer; silence and barge-in designed as events
Recognition errors dominate: separate ASR errors from NLU errors, word and slot error rate on real audio
Identifiers: vocabulary hints and constraints, check digits, read back in groups, keypad after one miss
Latency: endpointing and streaming, with real acknowledgements for slow tool calls
Separate thresholds and test sets from real audio; measure entity accuracy, escalation and completion per channel

say: I'd design the task twice, not port the chat flow. Voice can't be scanned, so prompts are short, the question goes last, and silence is an event I plan for.
I'd never trust a spoken account number without reading it back in groups, and after one miss I'd offer the keypad.
And I'd keep separate thresholds and test sets per channel, from real audio. Voice utterances aren't chat test data.
avoid: Quoting overall word error rate as proof the voice channel works

topics.title: Flows or a generative agent
topics.brief: Every platform gives you a router on top (which task does the user want) and deterministic state underneath (walk the task to completion); what changed is that the router can now be an LLM reading descriptions. Decide per task by risk: authentication, payments and anything regulated stay in deterministic flows, open-ended help goes to a generative layer with retrieval, and the middle gets generation with approval checkpoints. The nuance: generative selection gets unpredictable when two descriptions overlap, so the taxonomy matters more, not less.
points: Deterministic flows: authentication, payments, record changes; predictable and auditable, but every new capability costs authoring
Generative layer: FAQs and open help grounded in retrieval; covers the long tail with little authoring, harder to test and certify
Middle layer: generation with approval checkpoints and an explicit confirmation turn for risky tools
The model proposes, code authorises: server-side authorisation on every tool, so an injected instruction cannot reach an action
Widen on evidence: start deterministic on the money paths and grow the generative scope as evaluation data supports it
production: Dialogflow CX: flows for deterministic work like authentication or payment, generative playbooks for open-ended conversation; intent routes take priority over condition routes and event handlers

Rasa CALM: the LLM only turns the message into commands and the business logic stays in flows; Rasa's migration guide runs old NLU and CALM side by side behind a router and moves related skills together

Copilot Studio: generative orchestration, the default for new agents, picks topics, tools and knowledge by description and can chain several in one turn; Microsoft notes selection becomes unpredictable when descriptions overlap
Rasa claims up to 90% less build work with CALM: vendor marketing, not a measured result
OWASP's top risks for LLM apps include prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency

mcq.q: Which job in a bank assistant should stay in a deterministic flow even if an LLM routes the conversation?
o: Answering 'what is a Roth IRA'
Explaining the fees on a fund page
Executing a transfer between accounts
Small talk at the start of a call
Summarising the conversation for an agent
mcq.why: Money movement needs fixed steps, validation and confirmation that a model cannot skip. Informational answers can be generated from approved, retrieved content.

mcq.q: In Rasa CALM, what does the LLM do?
o: Writes the steps of each business flow at runtime
Turns the user's message into commands such as start flow or set slot
Executes the API calls inside each flow
Replaces all the flows with a single prompt
Retrains the intent classifier on new logs
mcq.why: CALM splits the work: the LLM interprets the user into commands, and the flow engine enforces the business logic. That is why the model never improvises the steps of a transfer.

mcq.q: Under generative orchestration, two topics have overlapping descriptions. What is the likely effect?
o: The planner always picks the first topic listed
Both topics run in parallel on every turn
The platform merges them into one topic
Topic selection becomes unpredictable between them
The planner falls back to trained intents
mcq.why: The descriptions are what the model chooses between, so overlapping prose is the old intent-overlap problem in a new form. Microsoft's docs say the choice then becomes unpredictable.

open.q: We have a classic bot with about 300 intents. How would you decide what moves to a generative agent and what stays in flows?
open.probe: Where you put determinism, and how you change a live system safely
a: Inventory intents by volume, success rate and risk
Keep accurate high-volume intents and every money or record-changing path in strict flows
Move the long tail and FAQs to retrieval or LLM routing, with server-side authorisation on every tool
Run old and new in shadow on logged traffic and compare on a golden set
Shift traffic gradually with a rollback, moving whole topic areas so related skills that interrupt each other stay together

say: By risk and determinism. Authentication, payments and anything with regulatory consequences stay in flows. Open-ended help and FAQs go to a generative layer with retrieval.
I'd start deterministic on the money paths and widen the generative scope only as the evaluation data supports it.
It's the same rule I use at alfred_: the model proposes, code authorises.
avoid: Quoting Rasa's '90% less build work' as a measured fact

modules.title: Intents, entities and dialogue state
modules.blurb: Model the understanding layer in the room: taxonomy, data, entities, state, thresholds, and where LLMs and tools fit in.

topics.title: The intent taxonomy
topics.brief: An intent is a unit of action the business can take, not a unit of topic: actions and queries are intents, and the information needed to fulfil them is entities. Split when the next step differs (a different flow, API, authentication level or compliance treatment); merge when fulfilment is the same and let a slot carry the difference. The nuance: over-fine taxonomies fail through overlap and imbalance, not through lack of coverage.
points: Action and object: cancel is one intent and the product is an entity; no 'cancel product X' intents
Merge or split: same flow and same API call means merge and use an entity; similar words but different handling (lost card against declined card) means split
Risk tier: informational, transactional and regulated intents get different thresholds, confirmation and off-ramps, so record the tier on each intent
Scale: past a few hundred intents, route by domain first (accounts, cards, loans, fraud) and classify within it, or use head intents with a modifier entity
Confusion matrix: off-diagonal mass between two intents means merge them, or split them properly with distinguishing data
Consistency: one schema style and hierarchical names (service.category.action) keep hundreds of intents navigable
production: Dialogflow CX trains intents only against others in the same flow, so splitting a big bot into flows reduces cross-topic confusion
Dialogflow CX guidance: at least 20 training phrases per intent, about 50 for the main ones, and no intent with far more phrases than its neighbours
Bank of America's Erica, as reported, grew from roughly 200 to 250 intents at launch to more than 700, each a curated answer or workflow
Fraud and 'I want a person' get top-priority routes from the start
With LLM routing, the descriptions of each flow or tool become what the model chooses between, so overlap moves from training phrases into prose

Past a few hundred I'd route by domain first. And I'd check it on real utterances with a confusion matrix before building any flows.

topics.title: Training data and out-of-scope
topics.brief: An intent is only as good as its training phrases: real users' words from logs, balanced across intents, varied in wording, with a held-out test set that is never trained on. Out-of-scope is two problems: politely declining what you never built, and never missing an in-scope but regulated request (a dispute, a fraud report) because it was phrased oddly. The nuance: the hard negatives are the ones that look like a supported intent, and the regulated detector is judged on recall, not overall accuracy.
points: Floors, not targets: Dialogflow CX recommends 10 to 20 phrases per intent, CLU warns under 15, Kore.ai asks 8 to 10, Cognigy's analyzer flags under 5

Quality: balance the classes (imbalance biases toward big intents), vary casing and punctuation, avoid accidental patterns like every example starting 'I want', and diversify wording instead of reordering it
Sources: production logs over designer-written phrases; LLM-drafted phrases only for a cold start, replaced as traffic arrives and never in the test set
Leakage: the same utterance or a near duplicate in train and test inflates the score
Negative intent: near misses ('buy a book' in a flight bot), greetings, yes and no, bare numbers, fed from real false matches in the logs
Regulated intents: a separate high-recall detector for disputes, fraud, complaints and hardship, tuned to over-trigger toward a human
production: Dialogflow CX scores intents from 0.0 to 1.0, fires no-match below the threshold, and has a default negative intent; Google warns it degrades past about 10,000 phrases and should be reviewed as some negatives become in-scope
CLU's None intent has a score threshold and replaces a top intent below it; Lex returns AMAZON.FallbackIntent when every intent scores below its threshold
The CFPB's 2023 chatbot spotlight flags bots that recognise a dispute only when specific words appear
Uncertainty-driven routing: a cheap classifier answers when confident and defers to an LLM only when uncertain, which improves out-of-scope detection without an LLM call on every turn

It means the speech model must be retrained
It makes the confusion matrix impossible to read

open.q: How would you make sure the assistant never misses a customer disputing a charge, however they phrase it?

Route on detection to the regulated flow or a human, before the bot attempts anything else
Feed misses back from logs and agent corrections; semantic matching helps catch paraphrases
Keep a human off-ramp in every state, because the escalation rule is a policy, not a prediction

say: I'd split out-of-scope in two. A polite decline for things we never support, and a separate high-recall detector for regulated intents like disputes, tuned to over-trigger toward a human rather than miss one.
I'd judge that detector on recall over real, oddly phrased examples, not on overall accuracy.
And the training data comes from real users' words. Designers write the way designers talk.
avoid: Quoting a platform's minimum phrase count as the target

topics.title: Entities: extract, resolve, validate
topics.brief: Extracting a value is the easy half. The real work is resolving it to something the backend accepts (a canonical id), validating it against business rules, and deciding what to say when it fails. The nuance: each kind of value has its own right extractor, and identifiers are matched deterministically against the system of record, never guessed by a model.
points: Extractor per kind: prebuilt for dates, numbers and emails; lists with synonyms for closed sets; regex plus validation for IDs; learned where context decides
False fires: a quantity entity built only on the prebuilt number fires on '3 PM'; CLU's fix is a learned component marked required
Roles: origin against destination needs a signal in the data, words like 'from' and 'to'
Resolve: restrict to listed values for anything that maps to a product or account id; expand only for fuzzy fields like 'reason for call'
Validate in code: amount within balance, date not in the past, account belongs to this customer, limit not exceeded, with a message specific enough that the next turn can succeed
Retry budget: a short prompt, a more specific reprompt with an example, then a menu, keypad or handoff
production: Lex V2 slots: a required flag, a different prompt per retry, a Lambda code hook that validates after each attempt; custom slot types either expand values (the default) or restrict to listed values and synonyms
Dialogflow CX extracts parameters only from annotated training-phrase spans, and can auto-generate up to 3 synonyms for list entities
Wells Fargo's Fargo, as reported, tokenizes and scrubs PII before the model sees the text, so the model gets intent and entity type but never raw account data
Copilot Studio's generative orchestration did not yet take custom entities (closed lists, regex) as topic inputs, so a Question node is still used for those

Expand, and let the backend reject it later

Neither; account type should be free text

open.q: A user says 'move 500 from my brokerage to the joint one'. Walk me through how the entities get from words to a transfer the backend will accept.

Resolve: 'my brokerage' and 'the joint one' map to ids from this customer's own accounts; if one matches two, ask a closed question
Validate in code: ownership, balance, transfer limits, with a specific message on failure
Retry budget then an exit, so a value that cannot be supplied ends with a person, not a loop
Mask account numbers in logs and transcripts at the extraction layer

say: I treat an entity as three steps: extract, resolve to an id the backend accepts, then validate against a business rule. Most bugs I'd expect are in the second and third steps, not the extraction.
At alfred_ we don't have an NER model. Contacts and events are resolved by deterministic code with thresholds, so 'the second email' maps to a real record or the assistant asks.
And every slot gets a retry budget and an exit.

topics.title: Dialogue state and how it is tracked
topics.brief: Dialogue state is the structured set of slot values and where the user is in the task, at each turn; tracking it means updating that record as the conversation goes. It is measured by joint goal accuracy, the share of turns with every slot right. The nuance: keep a compact state with real ids plus a short transcript window, rather than replaying the whole conversation and hoping the model reads it correctly.
points: Contents: active task, slot values, pending action, authentication status, ids of the things referred to
Joint goal accuracy: strict on purpose, since one wrong slot fails the turn, as a booking with the wrong date is a failed booking

On platforms: a Dialogflow CX page is a state whose form collects required parameters, prefilled from the session or the matched intent; Lex elicits slots through code hooks (ElicitSlot, ConfirmIntent); Rasa uses collect steps
With LLMs: often function calling, where each tool is an intent and its arguments are the slots
References: 'that one' or 'the ETF I mentioned' resolve to ids held in state, not to model memory
Caching: stable policy text and metadata can be cached; balances and execution status never, without a freshness rule
production: FnCTOD used function calling for zero-shot state tracking: 5.6 points of joint goal accuracy gained for ChatGPT and 14 for GPT-4
A router in front of the state is monitored with a confusion matrix, the top-two margin and calibration error; class drift and calibration decay are its failure modes
LLM planners can behave differently in a fresh session and a long one, so regression tests are scripted multi-turn transcripts

topics.title: Thresholds, margins and colliding intents
topics.brief: A confidence threshold decides when the assistant acts, confirms or falls back, and it comes from your own evaluation data, never a default. Use three bands, a higher bar for risky intents, and watch the margin between the top two as well as the top score. The nuance: scores are model-specific and comparative, so every model or training change means recalibrating, and a threshold change ships as a release.
points: Three bands: act above the high threshold, confirm or disambiguate in the middle, fall back below
From data: plot precision, recall and the cost of a wrong action against the threshold, per intent family
Risk: high-risk intents get a higher bar and an explicit confirmation on top
Margin: a small gap between the top two means ask, even when the top score looks high
Calibration: a model can be wrong at 1.00 confidence; temperature scaling corrects overconfidence, and recalibrate after every change

Colliding intents: when an FAQ and a transaction collide ('my card...'), the transaction wins with an action verb and account context, questions go to retrieval, and close scores get one line: 'card fees, or something with your card?'
production: Cognigy: accept above 0.4 by default, reconfirm between 0.2 and 0.4, not found below
Lex sets nluIntentConfidenceThreshold per locale and returns the top intent with up to four alternates; its docs say scores are comparative and may change as the models improve
CLU needs a retrain and republish after a threshold change, so a threshold change is a release
Keep an explicit 'needs a transaction' intent so retrieval never answers an account-specific question, and test on labelled near-miss pairs

Scores above 0.9 can always be trusted
Only the top intent's score should ever be used

Fall back, since both scores are unreliable
Average the two intents' flows

Lower the threshold so both can act

Underfitting; add more intents to the taxonomy

A threshold set too low; raise it to 0.999
ASR noise; retrain the speech model
mcq.why: If high scores are not right as often as they claim, no threshold helps. Calibration makes a 0.9 mean right about 90% of the time; raising the cutoff only hides the problem.

A higher bar plus explicit confirmation for high-risk intents; a margin check on the top two
Check calibration first, since an overconfident model makes any threshold meaningless
Recalibrate after every model or training change, and ship a threshold change as a release

topics.title: Classic NLU, an LLM, or both
topics.brief: It depends on the label space and the constraints: a fine-tuned encoder wins on a stable, labelled, latency-critical domain; an LLM wins when the schema changes, labels are few, or out-of-scope recall matters. Production usually runs a hybrid where a fast classifier takes confident turns and an LLM takes uncertain ones. The nuance: the LLM took over understanding while deterministic code kept ownership of action, and grounding means something different for an FAQ (retrieval), a balance (an API), a transfer (a confirmed flow) and compliance text (approved content).
points: Encoder: faster, cheaper and often as accurate on a stable labelled domain, with per-intent metrics
LLM: no training pipeline, switches schemas without retraining, better out-of-scope recall; slower and less deterministic
Router: send a turn to the LLM when the classifier is uncertain: a calibrated threshold, the top-two margin, or disagreement under Monte Carlo dropout
Four kinds of grounding: an FAQ by retrieval with a citation, a balance by an API call, a transfer by a confirmed flow, compliance answers by approved content
Thin intent layer: keep stable labels even behind an LLM router, for routing, compliance review and reporting
Adding an LLM safely: generative fallback or retrieval-backed FAQ first, a golden set and judge rubric before traffic, shadow then a small experiment, transactions stay in flows
production: Amazon (EMNLP 2024 industry track): routing to the LLM only when a SetFit classifier was uncertain stayed within 2% of the LLM's accuracy with 50% less latency; large label spaces hurt LLM out-of-scope accuracy

A 2026 preprint (one data point, not yet peer reviewed): fine-tuned RoBERTa beat Claude Haiku on ATIS, 95.9 to 84.1, and tied on CLINC150, but the LLM's out-of-scope recall was 85.6 against 58.1, at about 981 ms p50 against 2.4 ms
Bank of America's Erica stays on 700 plus curated intents; its CTO is reported saying a 98% non-hallucination rate is not enough for money movement
Wells Fargo's Fargo, as reported: the LLM only extracts intent and entities from PII-scrubbed text, the orchestration is model-agnostic, and it handled 245.4 million interactions in 2024
Dialogflow CX generative fallback on no-match sits outside the CX SLA, uses banned-phrase lists, and falls back to scripted text if generation fails

mcq.q: Which situation most favours an LLM over a fine-tuned encoder for intent detection?
o: A stable set of 30 intents with years of labelled logs
A voice IVR with a 50 ms latency budget
Intent schemas that change per client deployment, with few labels
A high-volume balance check with one common phrasing
A model risk team that needs per-intent metrics
mcq.why: An LLM switches schemas without retraining and needs few labels. Stable labels, tight latency and per-intent audit needs all point to the encoder.

mcq.q: In a hybrid router, what should send a turn to the LLM?
o: The message is longer than ten words
The user has been authenticated
The classifier's top score is above 0.9
The previous turn also went to the LLM
The classifier is uncertain: low calibrated confidence or a small top-two margin
mcq.why: The point of the hybrid is that the cheap classifier handles what it is sure of. Uncertainty, measured by calibrated confidence, the margin or dropout disagreement, is the routing signal.

mcq.q: A bank wants an LLM in its existing Dialogflow bot. What is the lowest-risk first step?
o: Let a playbook handle payments end to end
Generative fallback on no-match, or retrieval-backed FAQ answers
Replace all intents with one LLM prompt
Let the LLM write new flows from the logs
Route authentication through the LLM
mcq.why: Start where a wrong answer costs least and the money paths stay untouched. Evaluate on a golden set first, then shadow traffic and a small experiment.

mcq.q: What does grounding mean for a customer's account balance?
o: Retrieval from the FAQ knowledge base, with a citation
A confirmed flow with an explicit yes
Approved compliance text, reviewed in advance
The model never generates the number; it calls an API and phrases the result
A judge model checking the answer afterwards
mcq.why: Each kind of answer has its own guarantee. For an account fact the API is the source and the model only phrases it; the failure to guard against is a paraphrased or rounded figure.
