mcq.q: Which request should the advice-seeking route catch, even though it sounds educational?
o: 'What is a target-date fund?'
'How do I change my contribution amount?'
'When will my tax form arrive?'
'What does an expense ratio measure?'
'Is a target-date fund good for someone my age?'
mcq.why: Tying a product to the asker's own situation makes it personal. The other questions ask what something is or how to do a task, which is education or servicing.

mcq.q: A signed-in client asks 'should I sell during this downturn?'. Which response fits the boundary?
o: A personalised answer from the client's holdings, labelled 'not advice'
Approved education, a plain line that it cannot advise on a trade, and an offer of a licensed person
A refusal with no further help, so nothing could read as a recommendation
A neutral summary of what other investors did this week
A generated answer that passed a groundedness check against market news
mcq.why: A label does not turn a personal recommendation into education, and a bare refusal is the doom loop regulators dislike. Approved education plus a route to a licensed person serves the client and stays inside the line.

mcq.q: Why route advice-seeking with a deterministic rule rather than letting the LLM decide each time?
o: Rules always detect advice requests more accurately than classifiers do
LLMs cannot recognise indirect phrasing such as 'what would you do?'
Regulators prohibit any model from making a routing decision
A rule acts the same every run and can be tested and shown to compliance
Rules need no training data, so they cost nothing to maintain
mcq.why: Detection can use a classifier, but once advice-seeking is detected, the route is a rule. A model may route correctly once and not the next time, and one leaked recommendation is a firm communication with no basis.

open.q: A signed-in client types 'Markets are down 8% this week. Should I move everything to cash?' Walk me through what the assistant does.
open.probe: Whether advice is an intent with a designed path and layered checks, and whether you know who owns the line.
a: The advice-seeking intent fires; it was trained on real paraphrases, indirect ones included
Approved education only, such as long-term investing and diversification, and one plain line that it cannot advise on this trade
An offer of a licensed representative or the advice product; the route is a rule and carries the transcript and context
A check on any draft catches a recommendation, prediction or promissory wording that slips through; on failure, the safe answer and the handoff
The turn is logged for supervision, and the paraphrases sit in a red-team set whose leak rate gates release
Compliance owns where the line sits; I build the control and ask how they draw it

say: It doesn't answer the question as asked. 'Should I sell' asks for a recommendation, and that needs a basis in the person's whole picture the bot doesn't have.

So the assistant spots the advice-seeking intent, answers with approved education, says plainly it can't advise on a specific trade, and offers a licensed person. The route is a rule in code, so the model can't talk itself past it.
Where exactly education ends and advice starts is compliance's call, not mine. I build the control, and I'd test it with a set of paraphrases and an advice-leak rate before every release.
avoid: Claiming a disclaimer turns a personalised answer into education
Stating where Vanguard's compliance team draws the line; ask instead

topics.title: Guardrails, compliant answers and the record
topics.brief: Guardrails are layers around the model: input rails for injection and PII, retrieval rails for trusted sources, execution rails for tool calls, and output rails for groundedness, banned wording and leaks. A compliant generated answer is a chain: vetted content, grounded wording with disclosures attached by the system, an output check, and a record of every turn. The nuance: detectors miss novel attacks, so the design assumes some get through and limits what a fooled model can reach.
points: Five rails: input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output (NeMo Guardrails' names); input and output rails see the most use
Detectors are a speed bump, architecture is the wall: least-privilege tools, identity in code, no secrets in prompts, confirmation on consequential actions
Disclosures by the system: attached in code, never trusted to the model
Chat is a firm communication: supervised, held to Rule 2210 and retained; Rule 4511 sets six years by default in a format that meets SEA Rule 17a-4, which is why write-once storage appears
The record per turn: message, answer, retrieved sources and versions, model and prompt version, guardrail results, handoff; analytics get a separate copy with PII scrubbed
Cost: every rail adds latency and false positives; measure block rates per intent on real traffic and review blocked samples
production: Llama Guard (a fine-tuned Llama 3 8B classifier) screens prompts and responses; Meta's smaller Prompt Guard targets injection and jailbreaks and was reported to miss non-English text and simple obfuscation
Google Model Armor screens prompts and responses and can redact or mask sensitive data with Sensitive Data Protection templates instead of ending the session
Bedrock Guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety bundle topic denial, content filters, sensitive information and grounding checks; Vanguard's Virtual Analyst write-up names Bedrock Guardrails
Vanguard's Client-Ready Article Summaries generate the necessary disclosures with each summary: disclosures attached by the system
SEC 'AI washing' settlements in March 2024 (Delphia $225,000, Global Predictions $175,000): what a firm says about its own AI is regulated too

mcq.q: Hidden text in a retrieved web page tells the assistant to email the client's statement to an outside address. Which defence still holds if the injection classifier misses it?
o: A system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions in documents
An output rail that scans the reply for email addresses
The send tool needs explicit client confirmation and reaches only registered addresses
A second LLM asked whether the request looks suspicious
A longer list of banned phrases in the input rail
mcq.why: Detectors and prompts can be bypassed. A tool that cannot send without confirmation, and only to registered addresses, leaves a fooled model nothing to land on.

mcq.q: Why would a broker-dealer keep chat transcripts in write-once storage?
o: Chat is a firm communication, and records must be kept unaltered, six years by default
Write-once storage makes retrieval faster for the assistant's memory
It lets compliance redact transcripts that contain PII after the fact
Rule 2210 requires principal approval of each chat message before sending
It is needed so models can be fine-tuned on conversation history
mcq.why: Rule 4511 sets six years by default in a format that meets SEA Rule 17a-4, and write-once storage is the usual way to show a record was not changed.

mcq.q: Compliance finds a bad answer from six months ago and asks how it happened. What must the record hold to reproduce it?
o: The final answer and a timestamp
The user's message and the model's name
An embedding of the conversation for similarity search
The analytics copy with PII scrubbed
The message, answer, sources and versions, model and prompt version, check results
mcq.why: To replay a turn you need everything that shaped it. Without the sources, versions and check results you cannot tell which link in the chain failed.

mcq.q: A new topic rail blocks 6% of legitimate fee questions. What do you do first?
o: Remove the rail, since false positives hurt containment
Review a sample of blocked requests by intent, then tune on labelled data
Lower its threshold until the block rate is under 1%
Accept it, since over-blocking is always the safe side
Add a second rail to double-check each block
mcq.why: Guardrails are models with error rates. Look at what is blocked, per intent, and tune with data; blind threshold changes or acceptance both skip the diagnosis.

open.q: How do you keep a generated answer compliant, and what would you show compliance if they asked how a bad answer happened?
open.probe: The whole chain from vetted content to a retained, reproducible record, not one clever prompt.
a: Vetted knowledge: approved, owned, dated and permissioned; retrieval filters access and effective date
Generation from retrieved passages only, with citations; numbers from tools; disclosures attached by code
Rails: input for injection and PII, execution for tool arguments, output for banned wording, predictions and groundedness; a safe answer and a handoff on failure
Every turn retained immutably with sources, versions and check results, apart from a PII-scrubbed analytics copy
To explain a bad answer: replay the turn from its record, find the link that failed, and add the case to the regression set

say: I think of it as a chain, and the model is the smallest part. Vetted content, grounded wording with disclosures added by the system, an output check, and a record of every turn.
I'd assume a detector will miss sometimes, so tools are least-privilege and anything consequential needs a confirm. Then a fooled model has little to land on.
The record matters as much as the rails. You can only fix what you kept, which is why at alfred_ I built a scanner over real production conversations to find the genuine failures.
avoid: Saying every generated answer needs a principal's pre-approval; how Rule 2210 applies to chat is compliance's call
Calling a guardrail classifier the defence rather than one layer

topics.title: Release evaluation, monitoring and model risk
topics.brief: Before a release, a golden set from real conversations and a compliance red team are scored, and the safety categories are gates, not averages: a release cannot make advice leaks or unsupported claims worse. Model risk ideas (inventory, validation, monitoring, effective challenge) apply to the whole system, with model, prompt, retrieval, tools and guardrails versioned together. The nuance: SR 11-7 was replaced by SR 26-2 on 17 Apr 2026, which targets banks and puts generative and agentic AI out of its scope, so the firm's own governance and FINRA's guidance carry it.
points: Gates, not averages: advice-leak rate, unsupported claims, missing disclosures, over and under refusal, and account data before authentication at zero
Judge calibration: compliance reviewers label a sample, judge agreement is tracked per criterion and re-checked on any prompt or model change; judges show position and verbosity bias
One versioned system: model version, prompt, retrieval setup, tools and guardrails; pin vendor model versions and re-run the suite on any change
Explainability as traceability: cited sources, logged tool calls and the prompt version let a reviewer replay a turn; do not claim the model's reasoning is explainable
Monitoring: slice quality and escalation by cohort (language, accent, channel) and watch drift in inputs, retrieval and refusals
Reading a metric drop: segment by intent, channel and day first; a market event shifts traffic to intents that were never meant to be contained
production: MT-bench: strong LLM judges agree with humans over 80% of the time, with position and verbosity biases, so calibrate on your own labels
Morgan Stanley's adviser assistant used task-specific evals graded by advisers and prompt engineers, with daily regression checks (vendor-side and secondary accounts)
Vanguard's Head of AI/ML for Advice posting: no capability reaches production without a quantitative, repeatable evaluation baseline; it also names drift monitoring and Model Risk Management
FINRA's 2026 report asks for prompt and output logging, model version tracking, human review of results, and testing before and after deployment
Vanguard's 2026 letter: trained phone representatives up nearly 20%, and 85% of calls resolved in one conversation; people are part of the design

Yes, if the LLM judge rates the new answers as more helpful
Only after averaging safety and quality into one release score
No, a safety category is a gate and a release cannot make it worse
Yes, and fix the leaks in the following release
mcq.why: Averages trade a regulatory failure for convenience. Safety categories are gates compared against the last release; quality gains do not buy them back.

o: Nothing, since the vendor validated the model before release
Pin versions where you can and re-run the full suite before clients see the change
Re-validate only the prompt, since the model is out of your control
Wait for the annual validation cycle in the model inventory
Move to an open model, since vendor models cannot be governed
mcq.why: The system is the unit: a model change can shift behaviour as much as a prompt change. Vendor oversight means pinning and re-testing, not trusting the provider's own validation.

SR 26-2 extends SR 11-7 to cover generative and agentic AI explicitly
No model risk ideas apply to LLMs, since their outputs are not deterministic
FINRA replaced SR 11-7 with Notice 24-09 for broker-dealers

mcq.q: Containment fell 10 points in the week after a market drop. What do you check first?
o: Whether the NLU model needs retraining on market vocabulary
Whether the LLM provider changed its model that week
Whether the intent mix shifted toward intents never meant to be contained
Whether the fallback message wording should be friendlier
Whether the containment target should be lowered for the quarter
mcq.why: Rule out a mix shift before blaming the model. More balance, 'what happened' and withdrawal traffic can lower containment while the assistant routes exactly as designed.

open.q: We want to release a new version of the client assistant. What has to be true before you'd sign off, and how would a model risk reviewer see it?
open.probe: Gates on safety categories, a judge you have checked, and a system that is versioned and traceable.
a: A golden set from real conversations plus a compliance red team: advice paraphrases, prediction bait, data requests before authentication, injections
Safety categories as gates against the last release; accuracy and groundedness scored too
An LLM judge for volume, calibrated against compliance reviewers' labels, never the only gate
Model, prompt, retrieval, tools and guardrails versioned together, each change with its eval results and a rollback path
After release: sampling, drift and cohort monitoring, and real failures turned into new test cases

I treat the model, the prompt, the retrieval and the tools as one versioned system, because a silent model update can change behaviour.
On SR 11-7, as I understand it, SR 26-2 replaced it this April and puts generative AI out of scope, so I'd ask how your model risk team reviews LLM changes.
At alfred_ my loop is a failure scanner over real conversations and a replay bench of real turns, graded by a person.

Saying your own evals gate every commit automatically; describe the replay bench graded by a person

modules.blurb: Say how you would measure an assistant before and after release, what you would log on every turn, and how you would keep cost and latency down without a hidden regression.

topics.title: Evaluate each layer on its own terms
topics.brief: One blended score cannot tell you what broke. Production teams measure each layer separately: routing or intent, entities (span F1 plus whether the entity resolved to the right record), retrieval, grounding, task success, cost, and for actions the duplicate rate and confirmation compliance. The nuance: suites have two jobs. Capability evals start low and show headroom; regression evals sit near 100% and block a change when they drop, and a suite stuck at 100% has stopped telling you anything.
points: Why layers: when an end-to-end test fails, per-layer scores say whether the router, the slot filler, retrieval or the generator broke, and show where a swapped component moved
Entities: span F1 says the text was found; resolution accuracy says 'that meeting' became the right record, which is what the task needs
Actions: duplicate rate (a retry did it twice) and confirmation compliance (no side effect without an explicit yes) are measured, not assumed
Capability versus regression: capability suites show headroom; regression suites hold near 100% and gate changes; watch for saturation
Per-intent floors: put floors on sensitive intents (fraud, dispute, hardship) instead of one global threshold, because 95% overall can hide 60% recall on fraud
Golden set as an artifact: versioned, owned, labelled to a guide, refreshed from redacted production traffic, or it drifts away from what customers say
production: Anthropic's eval guidance: start with 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures, grade what the agent produced rather than the path it took, and read the transcripts.
Rasa's end-to-end tests assert on slots, responses and custom actions for each scripted conversation: the flow layer as tests.
DoorDash adds each issue it finds to a unit-test-like suite that runs on every prompt change (secondary summary).

At scale the hard number is tokens times concurrent runs times tool latency, not HTTP requests per second; downstream tool APIs are often the real bottleneck, so timeouts and bounded parallelism belong in the evals too.
Review sampling is ranked by volume times cost times severity: every escalation, abandonment, low-confidence route, negative feedback, failed tool call and long run, plus a random baseline.

mcq.q: Your regression suite has passed at 100% for three months while customers keep reporting new failures. What is the problem?
o: The suite is saturated and no longer covers what breaks
The model is overfitting to the regression suite
The pass threshold should be raised further
Regression suites should start low and climb
The graders are too strict about wording
mcq.why: A suite that always passes carries no information. Add the new production failures as cases, and keep a capability suite that still has headroom.

mcq.q: You add a suite of hard multi-step tasks and the agent scores 30%. How should you treat it?
o: As a regression gate that blocks every merge
As a sign the suite is broken and should go
As a capability eval that shows headroom
As proof the model must be replaced now
As a reason to lower the regression threshold
mcq.why: Capability evals are meant to start low and show progress. Gating merges on a 30% suite would block everything; tasks graduate to the regression suite once they pass reliably.

mcq.q: Entity span F1 is 0.96, yet requests about 'the second email' often act on the wrong email. Which metric is missing?
o: Intent macro-F1
Retrieval recall at k
Groundedness of the reply
Resolution accuracy to the right record
BLEU on the generated reply
mcq.why: Span F1 checks the words were found. The task needs the reference resolved to the right record, which is a separate layer with its own metric.

mcq.q: An end-to-end score drops after you swap the embedding model. Why do per-layer metrics help?
o: They raise the end-to-end score directly
They remove the need for a golden set
They make the judge more consistent
They let you skip the regression tests
They show whether retrieval or a later layer moved
mcq.why: With per-layer scores you can see that retrieval recall fell (or did not) and fix the right component, instead of guessing from one blended number.

open.q: We have one accuracy number for our assistant. How would you set up offline evaluation so it tells us what to fix?
open.probe: Per-layer metrics for diagnosis, two kinds of suite, and growth from real failures.
a: Split by layer: routing or intent per class, entity span and resolution accuracy, retrieval recall, groundedness, task success, cost per conversation.
For actions, measure the duplicate rate and confirmation compliance directly.
Two suites: a regression suite near 100% that gates changes, with per-intent floors on sensitive intents, and a capability suite that shows headroom.
Start with 20 to 50 cases from real failures and add every new production failure.
Version the golden set with an owner and a labelling guide, and refresh it from redacted production traffic.

say: I don't trust a single accuracy number. I'd measure each layer on its own terms, routing, entities, retrieval, grounding, task success and cost, so a failure points at a component.

For anything with side effects I'd measure duplicates and whether every action had an explicit confirmation. At alfred_ that's how the confirm flow works: a side-effecting tool returns a preview first, a second call with explicit confirmation executes, and idempotency keys make retries safe.
Then the suite grows from real failures, not from guesses.
avoid: Quoting an overall intent accuracy for alfred_: there is no trained classifier there to report one

topics.title: Simulated users and pass^k
topics.brief: Scripted test conversations only check what you scripted. A simulated user, an LLM playing a customer with a hidden goal, exercises multi-turn behaviour at scale. tau-bench showed how to score it: compare the final database state with the goal state, and report pass^k, the chance the agent succeeds on all k tries. The nuance: simulated users are friendlier and more articulate than real ones, so their pass rate overstates production.
points: State-based grading: if the task is to cancel an order, the backend either matches the goal state or it does not; a deterministic grader under a stochastic conversation
pass^k versus pass@k: pass@k is at least one success in k tries (fine when you can check and pick); pass^k is all k succeed, which matches a system that must be right every time
Reliability compounds: a 90% single-run rate gives 0.9 to the fifth, about 59%, for five similar customers in a row
Personas that stress failure: vague, changes mind mid-flow, pushes for something the policy forbids, angry, speaks in fragments, tries to get another customer's data
Grade policy as well as outcome: confirmation before a transfer, identity verified before details are shared, a handoff when one is required
Anchor: keep human-written and replayed real conversations; a simulator does not reproduce noisy ASR or real impatience
production: tau-bench (Sierra) pairs an LLM-simulated user with an agent that has domain API tools and a policy document, in retail and airline domains, and grades by comparing the end database state with the annotated goal state.
The paper reports strong function-calling agents of the time passed under half the retail tasks and had pass^8 below 25%.
Anthropic's eval guidance says conversational agents need a second LLM simulating the user, and that pass^k reflects consistency requirements better than pass@k.
For a finance assistant the state check reads: the right transaction, and only that one, staged; a confirmation step present; disclosures given; nothing written that should not have been.

mcq.q: An agent succeeds on a scenario 90% of the time per run. Roughly how likely is it to get five similar customers in a row right?
o: About 90%
About 99%
About 45%
About 59%
About 10%
mcq.why: Independent runs multiply: 0.9 to the fifth is about 0.59. A per-run rate that looks high still fails a lot of customers at volume.

mcq.q: Why does tau-bench grade the final database state rather than the dialogue text?
o: Dialogue text is too long to store
It is objective and cheap, whatever words were used
Judges cannot read multi-turn conversations
The state includes the user's satisfaction
Text grading would favour the simulator
mcq.why: Many different conversations can reach the right outcome. Checking the end state against the goal gives a deterministic grade without judging wording.

mcq.q: For a support agent that moves money, which metric fits the risk?
o: pass@k: at least one of k tries succeeds
Mean BLEU against a reference reply
pass^k: all k tries succeed
Single-run accuracy at temperature zero
Average judge score across the tries
mcq.why: A customer gets one try. pass^k measures whether the agent is consistently right; pass@k suits settings where you can generate several and pick a checked winner.

mcq.q: Your simulated-user suite passes at 92%, but production completion on the same flows is 75%. What is the most likely reason?
o: Production logs are miscounting completions
The simulator is too adversarial
pass^k inflates the simulated number
Production uses a different model by accident
Simulated users are more cooperative than real ones
mcq.why: An LLM playing a customer is articulate, patient and on topic. Treat simulation as a regression and stress tool, calibrated against real transcripts, not as a forecast.

open.q: How would you evaluate a multi-turn flow, say moving money between accounts, before customers can use it?
open.probe: State-based grading, reliability over k runs, adversarial personas, and the limits of simulation.
a: Simulated users with hidden goals and personas that stress the flow: vague, changing their mind, pushing for something forbidden.
Grade the end state and the policy: the right transfer staged only after explicit confirmation, identity checked first, a handoff when required.
Run each scenario k times with varied temperature and persona, report pass^k, and read the failing transcripts.
Anchor with replayed real conversations, because the simulator is friendlier than customers and has no ASR noise.
Read the simulated rate as a regression and stress signal, not a forecast of production completion.

say: For multi-turn behaviour I'd use a simulated user with a hidden goal and grade the final state and the policy, not the wording.
I'd run each scenario several times and look at pass^k, because a bot that succeeds seven times out of eight is still a bad bot at scale.
And real conversations stay the anchor. At alfred_ my replay bench runs over real production turns and a person grades it, because simulated users are more polite than real ones.
avoid: Reading a simulated pass rate as a forecast of production containment

topics.title: Calibrating an LLM judge
topics.brief: A judge model is useful only once you have measured how well it agrees with your people, criterion by criterion. The working pattern: binary or small-scale criteria with explicit definitions, the evidence given to the judge, a human-labelled calibration set, known biases controlled, and a human sample reviewed for as long as the judge runs. The nuance: judges reward fluent, confident, long answers, so a polished hallucination scores well unless the criterion forces a check against the source.
points: Criteria: narrow, checkable true or false questions ('every number appears in the retrieved passage or the API result'), not 'is this a good answer'
Calibration: people label the same conversations, you measure agreement per criterion and fix the wording or the judge; automate only the criteria where it matches
Biases: position (run both orders and require the same winner), verbosity (prefers longer answers), self-enhancement (judge with a different model family)
Pairwise over absolute: 'is B better than A' is more stable than a 1 to 5 score, and is the right tool for a ship decision
Reasoning first: ask for the reasoning, then the verdict, and convert to structured output as a separate step; low temperature, several votes on high-stakes criteria
Limits: never the only control on a regulated answer; that needs a deterministic check or an approved content library
production: Instacart's LACE scores five dimensions (query understanding, answer correctness, chat efficiency, client satisfaction, compliance) from binary criteria; a debate setup worked best on context-dependent criteria, and subjective ones like conciseness stay directional checks.
DoorDash's quality judge scores retrieval correctness, response accuracy, language, coherence and relevance, alongside human review of random samples to keep it calibrated.
The MT-Bench paper found strong judges reach over 80% agreement with human preferences, similar to humans with each other; Langfuse's guide cites 80 to 90% on many criteria.
In a control environment teams record the judge prompt version, the model version and human agreement by criterion, and send disagreements to a named reviewer.

mcq.q: In pairwise tests your judge prefers whichever answer is shown first 62% of the time. What fixes this?
o: Use a larger judge from the same family
Switch to a 1 to 10 absolute score
Ask the judge in the prompt to be unbiased
Run both orders and keep only consistent winners
Trim both answers to the same length
mcq.why: That is position bias. Swapping the order and requiring the same winner cancels it; trimming length addresses verbosity, a different bias.

mcq.q: Your judge rates long, confident answers higher even when they state an unsupported fee. Which change helps most?
o: Give it the source and require every number to appear in it
Ask for a 1 to 10 score instead of pass or fail
Use the same model that wrote the answer
Raise its temperature for more varied scores
Show it the answers in a random order
mcq.why: Verbosity and fluency bias let polished claims through. A grounded criterion with the evidence attached makes the judge check the claim instead of the tone; order shuffling fixes position bias, not this.

mcq.q: You must decide whether a new prompt beats the current one. Which judging setup is most stable?
o: Absolute 1 to 5 scores on each, compared by mean
One judge vote per conversation at high temperature
Self-rating by the model that wrote each answer
Counting which prompt gives longer answers
Pairwise comparison in both orders on the same conversations
mcq.why: Relative judgements are more consistent than absolute scores, and running both orders on the same inputs removes position bias and input differences.

mcq.q: The judge agrees with your people 90% on tone but 60% on policy compliance. What do you do?
o: Average the two and report 75%
Drop the judge for both criteria
Automate tone, keep people on compliance, rework that criterion
Retrain your people to match the judge
Use the tone score as a proxy for compliance
mcq.why: Agreement is per criterion. Use the judge where it matches people, and on the weak criterion tighten the wording or keep humans, especially when it is the high-risk one.

open.q: You want an LLM to score thousands of support conversations a week. How do you know its scores mean anything?
open.probe: Treating the judge as a model that needs its own evaluation.
a: Write narrow binary criteria with definitions, and give the judge the evidence (retrieved passages, tool results), not only the reply.
Have people label a few hundred conversations with the same rubric and measure agreement per criterion.
Control the biases: both orders in pairwise tests, a different model family, an eye on length.
Automate only criteria with good agreement; keep a human sample running and re-check when the judge prompt or model changes.
Never make it the only gate on a regulated answer; use deterministic checks there.

say: I treat the judge as another model that needs its own evaluation. I'd label a couple hundred conversations by hand, measure agreement per criterion, and only automate the ones where it matches us.
Where a check has to be exact I'd use code instead. At alfred_ claims of actions or searches are checked against the turn's tool-execution ledger, and that check is deterministic, not an LLM.
And I'd keep a human sample going, because judges drift too.
avoid: Claiming an LLM reviews each reply at alfred_: the action-claim check is deterministic code against the ledger
Quoting a judge agreement figure as your own result at alfred_

topics.title: Offline green is not online good
topics.brief: Golden sets are written by you, from yesterday's traffic, in clean text. Production brings new products, new phrasing, noisy speech and adversarial users. So evaluation continues after release: shadow mode, a canary, A/B tests on outcomes and sampled human review, with every finding flowing back into the offline set. The nuance: in a regulated firm you do not A/B test a new compliance answer on customers; content goes through approval first and experiments cover routing and presentation.
points: Three offline blind spots: selection (only what you thought to include), time (last quarter's phrasing), channel (text tests miss ASR errors, interruptions and silence)

Shadow mode: the candidate runs on live traffic, its output logged and never shown; compare intent, answer and tool calls with production and review the disagreements; costs tokens, carries no customer risk
Canary: 1 to 5% of traffic or one segment, with automatic rollback on guardrail metrics (fallback, handoff, complaints, latency, sampled judge scores)
Outcomes: containment read with repeat contact within 7 days, CSAT and cost per conversation; pairwise preference on sampled shadow outputs needs far fewer samples than a full A/B test
Automation rate: Intercom frames it as involvement rate times resolution rate, separating how often the bot gets a chance from how well it uses it
Close the loop: each reviewed failure is labelled and becomes a golden-set row, and often a new intent, guardrail or content fix
production: LinkedIn built tooling to evaluate on the order of 500 conversations a day for hallucination and responsible AI issues.
Langfuse describes the loop as online monitoring catching the edge cases the dataset missed, which are then added to the dataset.
Klarna reported a 25% drop in repeat inquiries, a better signal than raw chat share, though critics note it does not say how that was measured or how case mix was controlled.
The CFPB warns that containment can rise because reaching a human got harder, the doom loop, so containment is paired with repeat contact, complaints and abandonment after fallback.

mcq.q: You want to see how a new prompt behaves on real traffic without any customer seeing its answers. Which do you use?
o: A canary on 1% of traffic
Shadow mode, logging its outputs only
An A/B test with a small variant
The offline golden set
A simulated-user suite
mcq.why: Shadow mode runs the candidate on live inputs and discards its output, so you see real-traffic behaviour with no customer risk. A canary shows answers to real customers.

mcq.q: Shadow results look good. What does a canary give you that shadow mode cannot?
o: Lower token cost than shadow mode
Coverage of intents missing from the golden set
A way to skip the regression suite
Customer outcomes such as repeat contact and complaints
Deterministic grading of every reply
mcq.why: In shadow no customer sees the answer, so there is no outcome to measure. A canary exposes a small slice and lets you watch what customers actually do next.

mcq.q: A voice assistant passes its text golden set at 97% but does much worse on calls. Which offline blind spot is this?
o: Selection: the set lacks those intents
Time: phrasing has drifted since labelling
Saturation: the suite sits at 100%
Leakage: test items were in training
Channel: text tests miss ASR errors and silence
mcq.why: Typed test utterances do not contain misrecognised words, barge-in or dead air. Voice needs audio-level tests and its own online monitoring.

mcq.q: The bot is involved in 50% of conversations and resolves 60% of those. In Intercom's framing, what is the automation rate?
mcq.why: Automation rate is involvement times resolution: 0.5 times 0.6 is 0.3. Splitting it shows whether to widen where the bot is used or improve how well it does there.

open.q: Your new model beats the old one on every offline metric. Would you ship it? What happens between now and full rollout?
open.probe: Knowing why offline results do not transfer, and the online steps that close the gap.
a: Not on offline numbers alone: the set misses unknown topics, new phrasing and channel effects.
Shadow it on live traffic, review where it disagrees with production, and run pairwise preference on a sample.
Canary to a small slice with automatic rollback on fallback, handoff, complaints, latency and sampled judge scores.
Judge outcomes over enough time: repeat contact within days, not only containment.
Feed every failure found back into the golden set; for regulated content, approval comes before any live test.

say: I'd never promote on offline numbers alone. I'd run the candidate in shadow first, look at where it disagrees with production, then canary it behind guardrail metrics.
Whatever we find goes back into the golden set, so the offline set keeps catching up with real traffic.
For regulated answers I'd change content through approval, and experiment only on routing and presentation.
avoid: Treating a rise in containment as proof the new version is better

topics.title: What to log per turn, and what not to keep
topics.brief: You cannot analyse failures you did not log. The useful record is one structured trace per turn: the redacted utterance, intent with confidence and top alternatives, slots, state, retrieved ids, prompt and model versions, tool calls and results, guardrail verdicts, latency per stage, tokens, handoff reason and an outcome label. The nuance: in finance every field carries a privacy and retention decision, and an engineer's debug store is not the compliance record.
points: Per turn: ids and channel, redacted utterance, ASR confidence, intent with top-k scores, slots, state, retrieved document ids with scores, prompt and model version, tool calls with arguments and results, guardrail verdicts, latency per stage, tokens, handoff reason, outcome
One trace tree: OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions give a span per model call with operation, provider, model and token counts, plus tool and agent spans; still marked in development, so pin a version
Content opt-in: OTel keeps prompts and completions as opt-in events rather than span attributes, which keeps sensitive text out of indexed fields
Redact at the edge: mask account numbers, SSNs, card numbers and names with typed placeholders, so error analysis keeps the structure; measure redaction recall
Two stores: an observability store (short retention, redacted, wide engineer access) and a system of record (long retention, access controls, audit); mixing them is the common mistake
Decision provenance: log the prompt, model and content version on every answer, so you can say what source the bot relied on at that moment
production: Langfuse (open source, datasets, online judges on sampled traces), LangSmith and Arize Phoenix (OpenTelemetry-based) sit on top of traces; in regulated finance the deciding factor is often self-hosting or VPC deployment, not features.
Microsoft Presidio detects and anonymises PII with redact, replace, hash and encrypt operators, and states it cannot guarantee finding all PII, so controls are layered.
FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 says recordkeeping rules apply to AI-generated and AI-assisted records, and that chatbot responses to specific inquiries may be retail communications.
OTel attribute names include gen_ai.operation.name and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and output_tokens, with execute_tool and invoke_agent spans in the same trace.

The token counts for that turn
The intent confidence score
The session's CSAT rating
The content version and retrieved document ids

mcq.q: Why does OpenTelemetry keep prompts and completions as opt-in events instead of span attributes?
o: Events are cheaper to store than attributes
To keep sensitive text out of default capture and indexes
Because spans cannot hold any text
So that token counts are computed correctly
To make traces readable in any vendor tool
mcq.why: Span attributes are indexed and captured by default. Making content opt-in keeps customer text out of places with wide access unless you choose to keep it.

mcq.q: Engineers need transcripts to debug, and compliance needs a long-term record. What is the usual design?
o: One store with long retention and wide access
Raw transcripts in the debug store, kept a week
Two stores: redacted short-lived traces and a controlled record
No transcripts at all, only aggregate metrics
Only the compliance store, with full engineer access
mcq.why: Mixing the two either exposes raw customer data to engineers or leaves the compliance record thin when the debug store rotates.

mcq.q: Redaction replaces every amount and date with '***', and now wrong-amount bugs cannot be analysed. What is the better approach?
o: Typed placeholders that keep the structure
Stop redacting amounts and dates
Redact only in the compliance store
Ask reviewers to guess the masked values
Log amounts in a separate plain file
mcq.why: A typed token (an account number token, an amount bucket) keeps what error analysis needs while removing the sensitive value.

open.q: We're launching an assistant in our app. What would you log for each turn, and how would you handle privacy?
open.probe: A complete per-turn trace for error analysis, with redaction, retention and provenance thought through.
a: One structured trace per turn: intent with confidence and top alternatives, slots, state, retrieved ids, tool calls and results, guardrail verdicts, latency per stage, tokens, handoff reason, outcome.
Prompt, model and content versions on every answer, so any reply can be reconstructed.
Redact at the edge before analytics, with typed placeholders, and measure redaction recall.
Two stores: a short-lived redacted debug store for engineers and a controlled long-retention system of record.
Follow a standard such as OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, pinned to a version, with content capture opt-in.

say: I'd log every turn as a structured trace: the intent, confidence and alternatives, tool calls, latency per stage and the versions in play, so any answer can be traced back.
I'd redact at the edge before anything lands in analytics, and treat the raw transcript as a regulated record with its own retention and access rules.
At alfred_ the turn's tool-execution ledger is what my grounding check reads, so that log isn't only for debugging. It's part of the product.
avoid: Putting raw customer text in indexed log fields

topics.title: Dashboards and alerts that find real problems
topics.brief: Uptime and error rate are not enough for an assistant. The signals that catch real breakage are behavioural: fallback and handoff rate by intent, confidence drift, repeat contact, latency per stage at p95, cost per conversation and sampled judge scores. The nuance: slice before you aggregate. A global fallback rate of 8% can hide one intent that went from 2% to 40%.
points: Quality signals: fallback, no-match and clarification rates, handoff by reason, thumbs down, abandonment right after a bot turn, repeat contact
Model signals: the top-1 confidence distribution, the share below threshold, the intent mix; a mix shift is often a business event and an early warning for the business too
Latency: p95 and p99 per stage (ASR, router, retrieval, LLM first token, tools, TTS); p50 hides the pain
Slices: intent, channel, segment, release and prompt version, because the cause of a spike is almost always one of these
Alert design: baselines by time of day and weekday, relative change with a minimum volume, routed to the owner, each alert linked to its traces
Kill switch: turn one topic to a fixed fallback or a person with a flag, without a deploy
production: Judge scores on a sampled slice (5 to 10% is a common starting point) are trended over time with human spot checks; alert on a sustained drop over a window, not on single scores.

OTel token usage metrics, including cache variants, give cost signals without a separate billing pipeline: tokens per conversation, cost per resolved conversation, cache hit rate, share of traffic reaching the large model.
Safety signals: guardrail trips, blocked outputs, PII found in outputs, prompt-injection detections, and any answer on a regulated topic that did not come from the approved library.
DoorDash runs an online guardrail and an offline judge as two monitoring layers (secondary summary).
Finance incident path: contain (switch the topic off), assess how many customers saw it from per-turn logs, correct, and record.

mcq.q: Global fallback holds steady at 8% after a release. Why might you still have a serious regression?
o: One intent can spike while others improve
Fallback is not a useful signal for bots
8% is above any acceptable threshold
Fallback only moves with ASR changes
Global rates update too slowly to show it
mcq.why: Aggregates average away a local break. Slice by intent, channel and release before trusting a flat global number.

mcq.q: Average LLM latency is a stable 700 ms, but callers complain about long pauses. What should the dashboard show?
o: Mean latency per day
Total tokens per day
p95 and p99 per stage
Error rate per hour
Number of active sessions
mcq.why: The mean hides the tail. Per-stage high percentiles show which stage produces the long silences people remember.

mcq.q: Which alert rule gives the least noise while still catching real breaks?
o: Fixed absolute thresholds on every metric
Any single judge score below 3
Every guardrail trip pages the on-call
Relative change against a time-of-day baseline, with a minimum volume
A daily email listing all metrics
mcq.why: Time-aware baselines remove normal daily swings, relative change adapts to each intent's level, and a minimum volume stops tiny intents from paging people.

mcq.q: Within an hour the intent mix shifts sharply toward 'my transfer failed'. Who should hear first?
o: Only the ML team, so they can retrain
The platform and business owners: it may be an outage
Nobody, until the weekly review
Conversation designers, to add phrases
Compliance, to file a report
mcq.why: A sudden mix shift is usually a business event, here likely a payments problem. It is an early warning for the business, not a model issue.

open.q: Design the monitoring for our live assistant. What's on the dashboard, and what wakes someone up?
open.probe: Behavioural signals sliced by intent and release, and alerts that are actionable.
a: Quality: fallback, handoff by reason, abandonment after a bot turn, repeat contact and sampled judge scores; model: confidence distribution and intent mix.
Latency p95 and p99 per stage, and cost per resolved conversation with the share of traffic going to the large model.
Everything sliced by intent, channel, release and prompt version.
Alerts on relative change against time-aware baselines with a minimum volume, routed to the owner and linked to the traces.
Safety trips and regulated-topic answers go to risk, with a per-topic kill switch that needs no deploy.

say: I'd alert on behaviour per intent, not only uptime: fallback and handoff against a baseline, confidence drift, p95 per stage and cost per resolved conversation.
I'd slice all of it by release, so a regression points at a deploy, and every alert would link to the conversations behind it. The first move is reading ten of them, not guessing.
avoid: Alerting on averages: p50 latency and global rates hide the tail and the one broken intent

topics.title: Cost per resolution, and the levers that cut it
topics.brief: Most conversational traffic is a few easy intents, so the large model should be the exception: a cheap router or classifier first, the LLM only when needed, the stable prompt prefix cached, context trimmed. The number to defend is cost per resolved conversation, not deflection. The nuance: a cascade saves money only if the router is calibrated, because a confident wrong answer on the cheap path has nothing downstream to catch it.
points: Cascade: an embedding router or small classifier takes high-confidence known intents, and low-confidence or open-ended turns go to the LLM; tune the threshold on a labelled set and watch the share at each tier
Risky intents: a stricter threshold or a confirmation step whatever the confidence, since the cheap path has no second check
Caching: put the stable part (system prompt, policy, tool definitions) first and cache it; cache FAQ answers keyed on content version; never cache anything personal
Shorter context: summarise old turns, retrieve fewer and better chunks, trim tool output; input tokens dominate long conversations and slow the first token
Fine-tune: for a narrow, stable task with plenty of labels (routing, extraction); keep facts that change in retrieval

Cost per resolved conversation: count platform, content, QA, review and human handoff, not only tokens; check it against repeat contact, and keep protected intents (disputes, hardship) out of the containment target
production: FrugalGPT reports matching the best single model with up to 98% cost reduction by cascading, and notes model prices differ by up to two orders of magnitude.
RouteLLM's learned routers reported over 85% cost reduction on MT-Bench at 95% of GPT-4 quality, sending 14% of queries to the strong model, but only 45% on MMLU: measure on your own traffic.
On Anthropic, cached input tokens cost roughly a tenth of normal input while cache writes cost a premium; batch work is discounted, which suits offline judge runs but not the live path.

Klarna reported (company figures) two-thirds of chats handled in the first month and a 25% drop in repeat inquiries; critics note mostly level-one questions and unclear measurement, and in 2025 it began rehiring people for complex cases.

Intercom separates deflection (the AI answered, the customer may have left unhappy) from resolution (confirmed, or no return with the same question), and warns that vendors often count non-escalated chats as resolved.

topics.title: The voice latency budget
topics.brief: On a call people notice a pause after about a second, so endpointing, ASR, the model, tools, TTS and the network share one budget. Most of the delay is turn-taking and LLM time to first token, which is why streaming and a fast path for simple intents matter more than a bigger model. The nuance: a faster, smaller model saves milliseconds and may add errors on account numbers and amounts, so latency and accuracy are evaluated together.
points: Budget, as ranges to measure against: endpointing 150 to 300 ms, final ASR 100 to 200, LLM first token 300 to 600, TTS first byte 100 to 250, network 50 to 150; roughly 0.8 to 1.5 s in all
Stream every stage: partial transcripts into the prompt, tokens into TTS at the first sentence boundary; a stage that waits for the previous one loses the budget
Percentiles: p50 can be fine while p95 is a long silence, and callers remember the silences
Fast path: a router answers a balance or hours question with a template and no LLM call
Tools: a core banking call can cost more than the model; acknowledge, run independent calls in parallel, and time out with a graceful fallback
Turn-taking: wait too long and you add dead air, cut in early and you talk over the caller; give more patience while collecting digits, and support barge-in
production: The AWS Builder Center's 800 ms rule gives per-stage ranges for a real-time voice agent and stresses p95 over p50.

A cascaded ASR, LLM and TTS pipeline keeps a text checkpoint where you can apply guardrails, redact, log and require approved phrasing, which is why many financial deployments stay with it rather than speech-to-speech models.
Voice evals need audio test sets with noise and accents, with error measured on the high-stakes tokens (account numbers, amounts), not only overall word error rate.
Long history inflates time to first token on every turn, so teams summarise earlier turns and keep the stable prefix cached.

topics.title: Choosing the classifier: the ladder
topics.brief: There is no best intent classifier, only the best fit for labelled examples per intent, how often the labels change, and the latency budget. Climb from a TF-IDF baseline to embeddings plus a head, SetFit, a fine-tuned encoder or an LLM, and stop when the next rung stops beating the last on your held-out set. The nuance: most production systems end as a cascade, a small model for the confident bulk and an LLM for the uncertain slice, and that only works if the small model is calibrated.
points: Baseline: TF-IDF with logistic regression or a linear SVM trains in seconds on a CPU, is interpretable, and tells you how hard the problem is
Embeddings plus a head: a frozen sentence encoder with logistic regression or kNN; strong with little data, cheap to retrain, and a new intent is new examples

SetFit: fine-tunes a sentence transformer contrastively on pairs built from 8 to 64 examples per class (same class close, different classes apart), then fits a logistic head; a few examples make many pairs, and the encoder already knows semantics

Fine-tuned encoder: BERT, RoBERTa or DeBERTa with hundreds to thousands of examples per class give the best closed-set accuracy; DistilBERT or MiniLM when latency is tight; typically learning rate 2e-5 to 5e-5, 2 to 4 epochs

LLM: no training, copes with changing labels and out-of-scope, but costs latency and money per call; with hundreds of overlapping labels, embedding kNN shortlists candidates and an LLM or reranker picks

Structure: multi-class is softmax with cross-entropy; multi-label ('freeze my card and tell me my balance') is a sigmoid per label with its own threshold, or split clauses first; a hierarchy (domain, then intent) lets an unsure fine prediction fall back to the right domain
production: Casanueva et al. (2020), who introduced BANKING77: dual sentence encoders with a light classifier beat full BERT-Large fine-tuning at 10 or 30 examples per intent, trained in minutes on one CPU

A 2026 preprint: fine-tuned RoBERTa beat Claude Haiku on ATIS (95.9 against 84.1) and tied on CLINC150, but the LLM had far higher out-of-scope recall (85.6 against 58.1), at about 981 ms against 2.4 ms p50
An ACL 2025 industry paper sends only the uncertain turns from a cheap classifier to an LLM for out-of-scope detection on CLINC150 and BANKING77; its stated limit is the first stage's calibration

Encoder latency, in order of effort: truncate, dynamic padding and length bucketing, ONNX or TensorRT export, fp16 or int8, distil to DistilBERT or MiniLM; cache frequent inputs; measure p95 on the target hardware

Multilingual: a multilingual backbone transfers across languages (SetFit reports this), but keep a per-language golden set and thresholds; Dialogflow CX sets its classification threshold per language per flow

o: A prompted LLM on every request, since 50 examples is too few to train on
Full fine-tuning of BERT-Large straight away, as the most accurate option
A TF-IDF and logistic regression baseline, then embeddings with a head, moving up only when a rung wins on held-out data
Zero-shot NLI with each intent as a hypothesis, since it needs no data
kNN over mean-pooled vanilla BERT vectors, since it needs no training
mcq.why: The baseline costs minutes and sets the bar every later rung must beat. Zero-shot NLI needs 200 forward passes per query, an LLM per call breaks 30 ms, and vanilla mean-pooled BERT is poor for similarity.

mcq.q: Why does SetFit work with about 8 examples per class?
o: It generates synthetic examples with an LLM before training
Pairs from a few examples give many contrastive signals, and the pretrained encoder only has to bend its space a little
It prompts a large model with the examples, so nothing is trained
It trains only a logistic head and keeps the encoder frozen
It uses a much larger encoder than BERT, which memorises the classes
mcq.why: SetFit fine-tunes the encoder itself on same-class and different-class pairs, then fits a head. A frozen encoder with a head is the rung below it.

mcq.q: 'Freeze my card and tell me my balance' goes into a single softmax over intents. What goes wrong?
o: The softmax gives each intent 0.5 and the router runs both
Nothing, because the confidence threshold catches it
The tokenizer splits on 'and', so the model sees two inputs
The two intents cancel and the turn falls to out-of-scope
The softmax forces one winner, so one request is silently dropped
mcq.why: A softmax picks one class per input. Compound requests need a sigmoid per label with per-label thresholds, or clause splitting before a single-label model.

mcq.q: When does a cascade of a small classifier and an LLM fail quietly?
o: When the small model is overconfident, so wrong answers clear the bar and never reach the LLM
When the LLM is more accurate than the small model on hard cases
When most traffic is routine and the label set is stable
When the latency budget is loose enough for the LLM
When the small model abstains on too many turns
mcq.why: The small model's confidence decides who escalates. If it is miscalibrated, its confident errors ship. Abstaining too often costs money but is visible, not quiet.

open.q: You have 200 intents, 50 examples each, and some LLM budget. How do you build the intent model, and how do you decide when to stop?
open.probe: Judgement on the ladder: cheapest first, measured, with a plan for the uncertain slice.
a: A TF-IDF and logistic regression baseline in minutes, to see how hard it is
Sentence embeddings with a head, then SetFit or a fine-tuned small encoder; 10,000 examples is enough for fine-tuning
A stratified held-out set, macro-F1 and per-intent recall, and a none class from day one; move up only when the next rung wins
Read the confusion matrix: merge or clarify colliding intents
Cascade: the small model takes confident turns, the uncertain slice goes to an LLM constrained to the intent list

say: I'd start with TF-IDF and logistic regression, because in a few seconds it tells me how hard the problem really is. Then sentence embeddings with a head, then SetFit or a small fine-tuned encoder, and I only move up when the next one beats the last on a held-out set.
With 200 intents some will collide, so I'd spend real time on the confusion matrix, and the uncertain slice would go to an LLM constrained to the intent list.
To be honest, at alfred_ we don't have a trained intent classifier: intent comes from an LLM with typed tool schemas checked in code. So this is how I'd build it, not something I've shipped.

topics.title: Calibration and thresholds
topics.brief: A softmax score is a ranking signal, not the probability of being right, and modern networks are overconfident. Calibrate first so that 0.9 means right about 90% of the time, then set thresholds per action risk from held-out data. The nuance: calibration and thresholding are two different jobs, and both drift with traffic and with every retrain.
points: Calibration: of all predictions made at 0.8 confidence, about 80% should be right; Guo et al. (2017) showed modern deep networks are overconfident
Measure: a reliability diagram, and expected calibration error (bin predictions by confidence, average the gap between confidence and accuracy, weighted by bin size)
Temperature scaling: divide the logits by one scalar T fitted on a held-out split; the top class never changes, so accuracy is unchanged, but which predictions clear a threshold does change
Thresholds by risk: a greeting can act at a low score, a funds transfer needs a high one, and a middle band confirms first; choose operating points on a precision against coverage curve
Margin: if the top two intents are close, clarify even when the top score clears the bar (Rasa's ambiguity threshold)
Drift: refit T and re-tune thresholds after every retrain; watch the live confidence distribution and fallback rate
production: Vendor defaults are only starting points: Dialogflow CX's ML classification threshold is 0.3, Rasa's FallbackClassifier defaults to 0.7 with an ambiguity margin, and CLU lets you set a None score threshold
Microsoft's CLU guidance gives per-intent examples of about 0.40 for a greeting and 0.95 for placing a call, and notes a model can predict the wrong intent at 1.00
Rasa's two-stage fallback: ask the user to confirm the likely intent, then to rephrase, then hand off; showing the top two as quick replies turns uncertainty into one tap
Hendrycks and Gimpel: maximum softmax probability is a usable baseline for spotting errors and out-of-distribution inputs, but some of those inputs still score high

It falls, because confident correct answers drop below 0.5
It shifts toward rare classes, because they gain probability
It stays the same, because dividing every logit by one positive scalar keeps the top class
It rises on rare classes and falls on common ones

mcq.q: On a held-out set, average confidence is 0.95 and accuracy is 80%. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
o: It is overconfident; fit a temperature on held-out data, then re-tune the thresholds
It is underconfident; lower the thresholds to accept more turns
It is well calibrated, since accuracy is far above chance
Accuracy is the problem; retrain with more data before touching confidence
Switch the metric to macro-F1, which corrects overconfidence
mcq.why: Confidence above accuracy is overconfidence. Temperature scaling fixes the confidence without changing predictions; thresholds tuned on the old scores then need re-tuning.

mcq.q: A bank assistant handles 'check balance' and 'send money'. How should their thresholds differ?
o: One global 0.5 threshold, so behaviour is consistent
Lower for send money, because a missed transfer frustrates users most
A higher bar for send money with a confirm band below it, and a lower bar for balance
No threshold for send money, since a confirmation step runs anyway
The same threshold, with a separate temperature fitted for send money
mcq.why: Thresholds follow the cost of a wrong action. A wrong balance answer is cheap; a wrong transfer is not, so it needs a high bar, a confirmation, and a clarify band below.

a: Measure: a reliability diagram and ECE on a held-out split that includes real out-of-scope traffic
Temperature scaling fitted on a separate split: accuracy unchanged, confidence honest
Thresholds per action risk plus a top-two margin; the middle band confirms or clarifies
Look at the confident errors: often a taxonomy or label problem, or a missing none class for near misses
Refit after every retrain; monitor the confidence distribution and fallback rate

say: First I'd check whether the scores mean anything, with a reliability diagram on held-out data. Then temperature scaling, which keeps the predictions and makes the confidence honest.
Then thresholds by risk: a balance check can go at a lower score, a transfer needs a high one and a confirmation.
At alfred_ the confirm flow does that last part in code: anything that sends or deletes always previews and asks first, whatever the model's confidence.

topics.title: Out-of-scope detection
topics.brief: In a bank assistant the expensive failure is a confident wrong intent, not a missed one. Treat out-of-scope as a designed case: a none class trained on real near misses, a calibrated threshold, a distance signal, and an LLM or a person for the borderline band. The nuance: catching more out-of-scope costs some in-scope accuracy, so you choose an operating point; you do not remove the trade-off.
points: CLINC150 (Larson et al., 2019): 150 intents in 10 domains plus out-of-scope queries; classifiers did well in scope and poorly on out-of-scope

Three kinds: out-of-domain (weather, to a bank bot), in-domain but unsupported (a product you do not offer), in-scope but ambiguous; they need a redirect, a policy answer or handoff, and a clarifying question

Detectors: max softmax with a calibrated threshold (the baseline), an explicit none class (often the most reliable on near misses), distance to class centroids or kNN in embedding space, and an LLM judge for the borderline band

Negatives: mine real logs (small talk, other products, competitors, a bare 'yes' or number) plus near misses like 'I want to buy a book' in a flight bot; synthetic negatives alone under-represent customers
Measure: in-scope accuracy, out-of-scope recall and false-accept rate at a fixed in-scope accuracy, never one blended number
BANKING77: 77 fine-grained intents, 13,083 queries, one domain, so the hard part is confusable neighbours; the original has no out-of-scope split
production: Platforms: CLU's None intent with a score threshold, Dialogflow CX's default negative intent, Lex's AMAZON.FallbackIntent
Microsoft's CLU guidance: add near-miss false positives to the None intent
The 2026 preprint: the LLM's out-of-scope recall was 85.6 against 58.1 for a fine-tuned encoder, the main argument for routing uncertain turns to an LLM
Log every rejection and review a sample on a schedule: it shows where the model quietly fails, the unsupported requests are the product backlog, and model-risk reviewers ask for it

Anything borderline goes to an LLM or a person.
And I'd measure false accepts at a fixed in-scope accuracy, because in a bank the confident wrong answer is the expensive one.

topics.title: Metrics, imbalance, labels and the production gap
topics.brief: Accuracy lies under imbalance, so start with macro-F1 and per-intent recall, then apply the cheapest fixes in order: class weights, resampling of the training set only, per-class thresholds, focal loss. The nuance: the labels and the test set are usually the bottleneck, not the model, and a 92% test score that fails in production is mostly shift, leakage, or a test set that does not look like traffic.
points: Precision, recall, F1: of what I flagged, how much was right; of what was there, how much I found; F1 is their harmonic mean, so a lopsided pair scores low

Micro against macro: micro pools every decision (and equals accuracy for single-label multi-class), so big classes dominate; macro averages per-class F1, so every intent counts; weight by business cost where you can

Imbalance, in order: fix the metric; class weights; oversample or undersample the training set only, never validation or test; per-class thresholds tuned on validation (often the biggest win); focal loss, which down-weights easy examples
Labels: confident learning (out-of-fold predictions that confidently disagree with the label) surfaces bad labels; confusable intents are often a taxonomy problem, to merge or split

Test against production: distribution shift (new phrasing, new products), prior shift (a different class mix), leakage from near-duplicates across splits, and preprocessing that differs between training and serving

The loop: label sampled production traffic, dedupe before splitting, use a time-based split, keep a frozen golden set apart from anything used for sampling or tuning, and add uncertain production turns by active learning
production: Label errors in BANKING77 (ACL Insights 2022): over 1,400 of 10,003 training utterances, about 14%, flagged as possibly mislabelled; removing them raised F1 by about 4.5%
Microsoft's CLU evaluation guidance: read the confusion matrix and merge intents that are mistaken for each other, or add distinguishing examples
Long tail: reweighting, logit adjustment or balanced softmax, paraphrase oversampling, and few-shot methods like SetFit for tail intents; track per-intent recall
Spend the labelling budget where it moves the boundary: low-confidence or small-margin production turns first; an LLM pre-labels and people review where it disagrees with the current model

95% accuracy and very low macro-F1
Low accuracy and high micro-F1

Support-weighted F1
The mean of per-class recall
Precision on the largest class
Accuracy
mcq.why: Each wrong prediction is one false positive and one false negative, so pooled precision, pooled recall and micro-F1 all equal accuracy. That is why micro hides rare intents.

mcq.q: You oversample the rare class. Which data must keep its real distribution?
o: The training set, since duplicates always overfit
Only the rare class, undersampling the common one instead
The validation and test sets, which must measure the world you serve
Only the golden set; other evaluation splits can be resampled
None, as long as the duplicates are paraphrased
mcq.why: Resampling is a training intervention. Evaluation splits that are resampled measure a class mix that does not exist in production, and thresholds tuned on them are wrong.

mcq.q: Test accuracy is 92% but production quality is poor. What is the first thing to do?
o: Label a sample of production traffic and score the model on it, per intent
Retrain a larger model on the same data
Raise the confidence threshold on every intent
Train for more epochs, since it is underfitting
Recompute macro-F1 on the existing test set
mcq.why: You need evidence that the gap is real and where it lives. Every other option acts on the same test set that failed to predict production.

open.q: Your intent model scores 92% on the test set, but complaints say it is poor in production. Walk me through it.
open.probe: Debugging the offline to online gap with evidence, not guesses.
a: Label a few hundred production turns and score on them: is the gap real, and which intents?
Check shift: compare training and production embeddings, and the class mix
Check the test set: near-duplicates across splits, label noise, preprocessing that differs between training and serving
Check the metric: accuracy can hide rare intents, so look at macro-F1 and per-intent recall
Fix the loop: production samples into training, a time-based split, a frozen golden set, monitoring on the live mix

say: Most likely the test set doesn't look like the traffic. So I'd label a sample of real production turns and score on that first, per intent.
Then I'd check for near-duplicates leaking between train and test, and whether the text is cleaned the same way in training and serving.

The fix is a loop: real production cases go into training and into a frozen test set. That's the same lesson as our replay bench at alfred_, which is built from real production turns, not ones we imagined.
avoid: Resampling the test set to balance it: it then measures a world you do not serve.

topics.title: The representation ladder
topics.brief: Each rung of text representation closes a gap the one below left open: bag of words and TF-IDF count terms, static embeddings put similar words close, contextual embeddings give a vector per occurrence, and sentence embeddings compare whole texts. The nuance: the lower rungs are not obsolete; TF-IDF and BM25 still win when the exact term is the signal, and embeddings are indexes for finding candidates, not records of truth.
points: TF-IDF: term frequency in this document times the log of (all documents over documents containing the term); 'the' counts for nothing, a term frequent here and rare elsewhere counts a lot; blind to synonyms and word order
BM25: the same idea with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalisation; still the lexical half of hybrid search

Distributional hypothesis: words in similar contexts have similar meanings, so training a vector to predict its context puts similar words close; nobody puts the meaning in, it falls out of the objective

word2vec, GloVe, fastText: skip-gram predicts context words from the centre word (CBOW the reverse), and negative sampling turns the vocabulary softmax into a cheap binary task; GloVe factorises global co-occurrence counts; fastText sums character n-gram vectors, so it embeds typos and unseen words

Static against contextual: one vector per word type ('bank' has one) against one per occurrence computed from the sentence (ELMo with a bidirectional LSTM, BERT with a Transformer encoder); contextual costs a forward pass, static is a lookup

The map: rules, then statistical models on features (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, HMMs, CRFs), then neural sequence models with attention, then the Transformer (2017), BERT's pretrain then fine-tune, and LLMs; each step replaced feature engineering with learned representations
production: TF-IDF still fits product codes, error messages and jargon, where the exact term is the signal, and it is the baseline every classifier should beat
Rules and regexes still own narrow, high-precision cases such as account and routing number formats
Hybrid lexical plus dense retrieval with rank fusion often beats either alone
Generic embeddings know general similarity; a bank's idea of 'same enough' is taught by fine-tuning on positive pairs and hard negatives, deployed only if held-out retrieval improves

o: A general sentence embedding, because it captures meaning
Averaged static word2vec vectors for the query
Mean-pooled BERT, because contextual vectors handle rare tokens
A larger embedding dimension, which preserves exact strings
BM25 or TF-IDF, because the exact rare term carries the signal
mcq.why: A rare exact identifier is where lexical weighting shines and dense embeddings blur. That is the case for hybrid search.

mcq.q: Why does fastText handle the typo 'balence' when word2vec cannot?
o: It builds words from character n-grams, so the typo shares most pieces with 'balance'
It was trained on more data, including common typos
It reads the whole sentence with a contextual encoder
It normalises spelling before training
It factorises a co-occurrence matrix that smooths rare words
mcq.why: word2vec only has vectors for words seen in training. fastText composes a word from its n-grams, so unseen and misspelled words still get sensible vectors. Factorising co-occurrence is GloVe.

mcq.q: 'Card' appears in 'my card was declined' and 'send a birthday card'. Which representation gives the two uses different vectors?
o: word2vec skip-gram with a larger window
GloVe, which uses global co-occurrence
A contextual model like BERT, which computes a vector per occurrence
TF-IDF, which weights the word by its rarity in each document
fastText, through its character n-grams
mcq.why: Static methods give one vector per word type, whatever the context. Contextual models compute each occurrence's vector from the surrounding sentence.

open.q: Give me the map of text representations, and tell me when the old ones are still the right tool.
open.probe: Breadth with judgement: why each rung exists and where it still wins.
a: Counts: bag of words and TF-IDF, BM25 for retrieval; cheap, interpretable, exact terms
Static embeddings (word2vec, GloVe, fastText): similar words close, learned from predicting context; one vector per word
Contextual (ELMo, BERT): a vector per occurrence; sentence embeddings trained to compare whole texts
The old rungs still win on exact identifiers, jargon and small data, and as the lexical half of hybrid search
Example: MetaRAG's TF-IDF weighted embeddings reached 82.5% precision against a 73.3% baseline

say: I think of it as a ladder. TF-IDF counts words, weighted by how rare they are. word2vec learns that words used in similar places mean similar things. BERT gives each word a vector from its sentence, and sentence embeddings let you compare whole texts.
The lower rungs still win when the exact word matters, like an error code, which is why I'd usually run hybrid search.
In MetaRAG, TF-IDF weighted embeddings got 82.5% precision against a 73.3% baseline.
avoid: Explaining exactly how MetaRAG weighted the embeddings unless you have checked the code first.

topics.title: Sentence embeddings and similarity
topics.brief: A useful sentence vector has to be trained for comparison. Mean-pooled BERT is poor because BERT learned to fill masked tokens and its vectors crowd into a narrow cone; Sentence-BERT and contrastive training (InfoNCE with in-batch and hard negatives) make cosine meaningful. The nuance: on unit-length vectors, cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance rank the same, so normalise once and use the cheapest, unless the model card says length carries meaning.
points: Why not mean-pool BERT: masked-token training is not a comparison objective, and the vectors are anisotropic (packed into a narrow cone), so almost every cosine is high

Bi-encoder against cross-encoder: Sentence-BERT encodes each text once with a siamese network, so finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences drops from about 65 hours with a BERT cross-encoder to about 5 seconds; the cross-encoder reads both texts together, slower but more precise, which makes it the reranker
InfoNCE: for each query, a softmax over its similarity to one positive and many negatives, each divided by a temperature (often around 0.05 to 0.1); the loss is minus the log of the positive's share
Negatives: in-batch negatives (the other examples' positives) are free, so bigger batches help; hard negatives, similar but wrong, help most; for intents, utterances from the most-confused intent

SimCSE and Matryoshka: SimCSE uses dropout noise as the augmentation and spreads the vectors out; Matryoshka training makes the first k dimensions useful on their own, so vectors can be truncated and renormalised
Similarity: cosine is the dot product with the lengths divided out; for unit vectors, squared Euclidean distance is 2 minus 2 times the cosine, so all three rank the same
production: Sentence Transformers' MultipleNegativesRankingLoss is the standard in-batch-negatives loss for fine-tuning on (query, positive) pairs, optionally wrapped in MatryoshkaLoss
Cohere Embed v3 requires an input_type (search_document, search_query, classification, clustering) and warns that classification and clustering vectors should not be mixed with retrieval ones
Retrieve then rerank: a bi-encoder fetches the top candidates fast and a cross-encoder reorders them, which is where negation and fine detail get fixed
Normalise at write time and use inner product in the index
