o: Mean pooling normalises every vector to unit length
BERT's vocabulary is too small to separate meanings
Cosine is the wrong metric; Euclidean distance would separate them
Its vectors sit in a narrow cone, because it was never trained to compare sentences
Position embeddings dominate the average
mcq.why: Masked-token training does not shape the space for comparison, and the vectors are anisotropic. Changing the metric does not help; contrastive training does.

mcq.q: Why do larger batches usually help contrastive training with in-batch negatives?
o: Gradients average over more positives, which cancels the temperature
Each query is compared with more negatives, including harder ones, at no extra encoding cost
Each positive pair is seen more times per epoch
Batch normalisation statistics become exact
The loss can skip the softmax with enough examples
mcq.why: Every other example's positive is a negative for this query, so a batch of N gives N minus 1 negatives for free. More negatives means more chances to meet hard ones.

mcq.q: Your vectors are L2-normalised. Which metric should the index use?
o: Inner product, since on unit vectors it equals cosine and ranks like Euclidean distance
Euclidean, because it is the only true distance
Cosine, because inner product ignores direction
Manhattan distance, because it is robust to outliers
It depends on the length of the query
mcq.why: For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine, and squared distance is 2 minus 2 times the cosine, so the ranking is identical and the dot product is the cheapest.

mcq.q: Searching 2 million help passages per query: bi-encoder or cross-encoder?
o: A cross-encoder over all passages, as it is the most accurate
A bi-encoder only, because cross-encoders cannot score pairs
A cross-encoder to build the index and a bi-encoder to rerank
Neither; only TF-IDF scales to millions
A bi-encoder to retrieve, then a cross-encoder to rerank the top few dozen
mcq.why: Bi-encoder vectors are computed once and searched fast; a cross-encoder must run per pair, so it only sees the shortlist, where its precision pays off.

open.q: Why can't you mean-pool BERT for sentence similarity, and how would you train embeddings that understand our banking intents?
open.probe: Depth on contrastive training and on what a hard negative is for an assistant.
a: BERT learned to fill masked tokens, not to compare; its vectors crowd into a cone, so cosines are all high
Sentence-BERT: a siamese encoder trained on pairs, each text encoded once
Contrastive training with InfoNCE: pull the query and its positive together, push the rest of the batch away; the temperature sets how sharp
For banking intents: positives are utterances of the same intent; hard negatives come from the intent it is most confused with
Normalise vectors; keep the model only if held-out retrieval or kNN macro-F1 improves

say: BERT was trained to fill in blanks, not to compare sentences, so if you average its vectors almost everything looks similar.

The fix is contrastive training: pull a sentence and its match together and push the rest of the batch away. For banking intents I'd use same-intent utterances as positives, and the hard negatives would come from the intent it's most often confused with.
Then I'd keep it only if held-out retrieval actually improves.
avoid: Saying Euclidean and cosine give different rankings on normalised vectors: they do not.

topics.title: Choosing an embedding model, and where it fails
topics.brief: Shortlist from MTEB, then decide on 100 to 300 of your own labelled queries, because leaderboard rank barely predicts domain results; FinMTEB found it a poor predictor for finance. The nuance: embeddings are weak on negation, numbers, IDs and domain terms, and in a bank the governance questions (where customer text goes, which model version, who validated it) often decide before accuracy does.
points: MTEB: the standard benchmark (8 task types, 58 datasets and 112 languages in the original paper, larger since); filter to your task and language, check it live, and never quote ranks from memory
Practical filters: maximum input length, dimension and storage, licence, hosting, latency, price, and whether the model needs query and document prefixes or input types
Your own eval: 100 to 300 real query-to-answer pairs; recall@k and MRR for retrieval, kNN macro-F1 for intents; small leaderboard gaps rarely survive
Failure modes: negation ('I can't log in' sits near 'I can log in'), numbers and identifiers, domain vocabulary, short queries against long passages, silent truncation when chunking
Mitigations, cheapest first: hybrid BM25 plus dense, a cross-encoder reranker, query rewriting, metadata filters, then domain fine-tuning with hard negatives
Finance: FinBERT is a sentiment model (BERT further trained on financial text and tuned on Financial PhraseBank), not an intent classifier; domain-adapted embeddings do help on finance tasks
production: FinMTEB (64 finance datasets): general MTEB rank was a poor predictor of finance performance, and finance-adapted models like Fin-E5 beat their general bases

Storage: OpenAI text-embedding-3 and Voyage models are Matryoshka-trained, so vectors can be truncated; Voyage reports int8 at 1024 dimensions within 0.31% of float at 2048 with 8 times less storage (vendor-reported); re-test your hard queries after truncating

Governance: FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 says existing rules apply whether a firm builds a model or uses a third party's; SR 11-7 style model risk treats vendor models as components to inventory and validate

Data handling: redact or tokenise account numbers and personal data before any hosted embedding call; prefer self-hosted or private deployments with no-retention terms, confirmed with security and legal

The embedding model's temperature is too high
The tokenizer drops the word 'not'

FinBERT is a financial sentiment model, at best a domain-adapted backbone to fine-tune, not a ready intent model
FinBERT only handles Chinese text
FinBERT cannot be self-hosted
No issue; it was trained on BANKING77 intents

open.q: How would you choose an embedding model for intent routing and FAQ retrieval at a firm like Vanguard?
open.probe: A method, not a leaderboard rank, with the finance and governance constraints.
a: Shortlist 3 or 4 from MTEB for the task and language
Filter on input length, dimension, licence, hosting, latency, price, and where customer text may go
Build 100 to 300 labelled queries from real traffic; compare recall@k, MRR and kNN macro-F1
Test the failure cases on purpose: negation, amounts, fund names and tickers, jargon
If weak: hybrid search and a reranker first, domain fine-tuning with hard negatives after

say: I wouldn't take it off the leaderboard. I'd shortlist a few, then test them on a few hundred real queries from our own traffic, because finance text has jargon and boilerplate the benchmarks barely test.
I'd deliberately test negation, amounts and fund names, since that's where embeddings blur.
And before any of that I'd ask where customer text is allowed to go, because that alone can rule out a hosted model.
avoid: Quoting MTEB ranks or a vendor's current best model from memory.

topics.title: Vector search, routing, discovery and drift
topics.brief: In an assistant one embedding layer does several jobs: nearest-neighbour search for retrieval, semantic routing in front of the LLM, and clustering missed turns to find new intents. The nuance: a router is still a classifier, so it needs per-route thresholds and regression tests, and changing the embedding model invalidates every stored vector and every threshold tuned on them.
points: Index choice: flat (exact) to about a million vectors; HNSW, a layered proximity graph searched by greedy descent, high recall and speed at high memory (knobs M, efConstruction, efSearch); IVF, k-means cells of which nprobe are searched; PQ, short codes per sub-vector for 10 to 50 times less memory; IVF-PQ for billions
Semantic routing: embed example utterances per route, send a query to the nearest route above a similarity threshold, otherwise to a default or a clarifier; fast, deterministic and auditable
Router limits: negation, entity-dependent meaning, and context-dependent replies like 'yes' or 'the second one', which must be read against the last question before routing

Intent discovery: embed logs, reduce with UMAP, cluster with HDBSCAN (no cluster count needed, and it marks noise), have an LLM name the clusters, and a person approves an intent only if one flow can serve every member
Dedupe: near-duplicate utterances inflate head intents and leak across splits, so dedupe by embedding similarity before splitting

Model changes and drift: vectors from different models are not comparable even at the same dimension, so re-embed into a parallel index, compare recall on a golden set, then cut over; monitor live embeddings against a reference window
production: semantic-router (Aurelio Labs): routes defined by example utterances and matched by cosine similarity, skipping an LLM call for the routing decision; keep utterance sets versioned and tested against a frozen regression set, since one loose example can steal a neighbour's traffic

Intercom's Fin team (vendor-reported): extract the key question with a small LLM, embed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, UMAP then HDBSCAN, recursive clustering and LLM naming; new conversations below 0.5 similarity to every centroid are flagged as emerging; clustering choices mattered more than the embedding model
Evidently compared five embedding-drift methods and recommends a classifier-based ROC AUC (train a model to tell reference from current embeddings; near 0.5 means no shift) as the default

pgvector is fine to a few million vectors and keeps the data in your database; dedicated engines add scale and filtering; measure recall@k against exact search on your data, then pick the cheapest index that holds it

Shrink the PQ code size
Raise efSearch, widening the candidate list at query time
Lower M, so the graph gets sparser
Switch the metric from cosine to dot product

mcq.q: In an IVF index, what does nprobe control?

How many cells the space is split into at build time

Add 'yes' as an example utterance on the cancel-transfer route
Lower the router threshold so 'yes' reaches more routes
Use a bigger embedding model that understands 'yes'
Treat 'yes' as out-of-scope and ask the user to rephrase

mcq.q: You upgrade the embedding model. What must happen to the existing vectors?

Re-embed only new documents; old vectors stay comparable
Rescale the old vectors to unit length to align the spaces
Re-embed everything into a parallel index, check recall on a golden set, cut over, and re-tune thresholds
Average old and new vectors during a transition window

open.q: Design how embeddings are used across a bank's virtual assistant, and how you keep them healthy over time.
open.probe: Whether you see the router, retrieval and discovery as classifiers and as dependencies with versions.

Retrieval: hybrid BM25 plus dense, flat or HNSW to start, entitlement filters, a reranker
Discovery: cluster missed and fallback turns weekly with HDBSCAN; a person approves new intents
Hygiene: versioned utterance sets and a frozen regression set; dedupe before splitting
The model is a pinned dependency: parallel re-embed and a golden-set check before cutover; monitor drift and fallback rate

say: I'd use one embedding layer for three jobs: a fast router in front of the LLM, retrieval for the knowledge answers, and clustering missed turns to find new intents.

The router is still a classifier, so it gets per-route thresholds and a regression set, and a bare 'yes' gets read against the last question before it goes anywhere. That's close to the entity resolution I built at alfred_: 'that meeting' resolves to a real record kept outside the model.
And I treat the embedding model as a pinned dependency: an upgrade means re-embedding into a parallel index and checking recall before cutting over.
avoid: Saying a semantic router is not a classifier: it is nearest-neighbour classification and needs the same thresholds and tests.

topics.title: Attention and the square root of d_k
topics.brief: Attention builds each token's new vector as a weighted mix of every token's value, with the weights coming from how well its query matches each key, for all positions in one parallel step. The nuance people miss: dividing the scores by √d_k is a variance fix. Without it, scores grow with dimension, the softmax saturates to near one-hot and the gradients vanish.
points: Q, K and V: each token's vector is multiplied by three learned matrices into a query (what am I looking for), a key (what do I contain) and a value (what I hand over if chosen)

The operation: softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V; one query is scored against every key by dot product, the softmax turns that row of scores into weights that sum to 1, and the output is the weighted sum of the values

Why √d_k: if query and key entries are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product over d_k dimensions has variance d_k and standard deviation √d_k; dividing by √d_k brings the scores back to unit variance

Saturation: large scores push the softmax to near one-hot, where its gradients are close to zero and learning stalls; dividing by d_k instead would overshoot (variance 1/d_k), leaving the weights near uniform
Self against cross: self-attention takes Q, K and V from one sequence; cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder output (translation, T5)

Causal mask: scores for positions after i are set to minus infinity before the softmax, so token i sees only the past; that is what lets one training sequence act as many next-token predictions at once
production: The original Transformer: d_model 512 and 8 heads, so d_k = 64 and every score is divided by 8
GPT-3 175B: 96 heads of 128 dimensions, so its scale is 1/√128, about 0.088
Cost: the score matrix is n by n per head and per layer, which is why long context is expensive (see the KV cache topic)

mcq.q: Why are attention scores divided by √d_k before the softmax?
o: So that each row of attention weights sums to exactly 1
To keep the dot products near unit variance so the softmax does not saturate
To make attention cost grow linearly with sequence length
To cancel the scale added by the residual connection
To keep each value vector at unit length before the weighted sum
mcq.why: Dot products of d_k-dimensional unit-variance vectors have variance d_k. Large scores push the softmax to near one-hot with tiny gradients; dividing by the standard deviation √d_k restores unit variance. The softmax itself makes rows sum to 1.

mcq.q: A colleague divides the scores by d_k instead of √d_k, with d_k = 128. What happens?
o: Nothing, because the softmax is unchanged when all scores are scaled
The softmax saturates to one-hot sooner and gradients vanish
The causal mask stops working because masked scores are no longer minus infinity
Scores shrink toward zero, weights go near uniform and attention loses selectivity
Training speeds up because the gradients through the softmax get larger
mcq.why: Dividing by d_k leaves variance 1/d_k, so every score is close to zero and the softmax spreads weight almost evenly. Softmax is invariant to adding a constant, not to scaling.

mcq.q: Which change to every score in one row leaves the attention weights exactly unchanged?
o: Adding the same constant to every score
Multiplying every score by the same positive constant
Dividing every score by √d_k
Squaring every score before the softmax
Replacing the largest score with zero
mcq.why: exp(s + c) factors out as exp(c), which cancels in the normalisation. Scaling changes how peaked the distribution is, which is exactly why the √d_k factor matters.

open.q: Draw attention for me, then tell me why the scores are divided by the square root of d_k.
open.probe: Whether you know the mechanism and the reason for the scale, not only the formula.
a: Project each token into a query, a key and a value with three learned matrices
Score one query against every key by dot product, softmax the row into weights, output the weighted sum of values; every position does this in parallel
With unit-variance entries, a dot product over d_k dimensions has variance d_k, so scores grow with dimension
Big scores saturate the softmax into near one-hot, where gradients are tiny; dividing by √d_k, the standard deviation, restores unit variance
Example: the original paper used d_k = 64, so every score is divided by 8

say: I think of attention as a soft lookup. Each token asks with its query, every token answers with its key, and the softmax decides how much of each value to take.
The square root of d_k is there because dot products grow with dimension, and a softmax fed big numbers goes almost one-hot and stops learning.
I built a Transformer from scratch for English to German translation at UIC, so this is the part I'm happiest to draw.
avoid: Saying the scale normalises the weights to sum to one: that is the softmax's job.
Calling attention linear in length: the score matrix is n by n.

topics.title: Inside one block: heads, position, norms, feed-forward
topics.brief: A Transformer is one block repeated N times: normalise, attend, add the input back; normalise, a feed-forward network on each token, add back. Several heads track several relations at the cost of one, and position has to be injected because attention ignores order. The nuance: about two thirds of a layer's parameters sit in the feed-forward network, not in attention.
points: Multi-head: h attentions run in parallel on d_k = d_model / h dimensions, are concatenated and projected by W_O; about the same parameters and compute as one full-width head, with each head free to learn a different relation
Position: attention by itself is order-blind, so position is added: sinusoids summed into the embeddings (the original), learned absolute vectors (BERT up to 512, GPT-2 up to 1,024), or RoPE

RoPE: rotates pairs of dimensions in each query and key by an angle proportional to position, with a different frequency per pair, so their dot product depends only on relative distance; applied to Q and K (not V) in every layer; the default in Llama-style models; going past the trained length needs frequency scaling, it is not free

Residual and norm: each sublayer adds its output back to x; the original put the norm after the add (post-LN) and needed learning-rate warmup; pre-LN normalises before the sublayer and trains stably without it (Xiong et al., 2020); many LLMs use RMSNorm, which drops the mean subtraction

Feed-forward: per token, expand to about 4 times d_model, a nonlinearity, project back; that is 8 d² of the roughly 12 d² parameters per layer, so about two thirds; Llama-style models use a gated variant, SwiGLU

Rough sizes: 12 × layers × d_model² ignores embeddings; GPT-3, 96 layers at 12,288, gives about 174B against the published 175B; BERT-base is 12 layers, 768 hidden, 12 heads, about 110M with its embeddings
production: Llama 2 7B: 32 layers, d_model 4096, 32 heads of 128, pre-norm with RMSNorm, RoPE and SwiGLU
Long-context versions of RoPE models (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) rescale the rotation frequencies and then fine-tune briefly on longer text
Budget arithmetic: training compute is about 6 × parameters × tokens; inference is about 2 × parameters per generated token

read.label: Su et al.: RoFormer, rotary position embedding
read.why: Where RoPE comes from and why the score depends on relative position.

read.label: Xiong et al.: On layer normalization in the Transformer architecture
read.why: Why pre-LN trains without warmup.

read.label: 3Blue1Brown: How might LLMs store facts
read.why: The feed-forward block, where most parameters live.

mcq.q: Splitting one 512-wide attention into 8 heads of 64 mainly buys what?
o: Eight times the parameters, which is where the extra quality comes from
Linear cost in length, because each head reads one eighth of the tokens
Several relations attended at once, at about the same parameters and compute
No need for position information, because heads specialise by position
A separate feed-forward network per head, which adds capacity
mcq.why: Each head works on d_model / h dimensions, so the projections total the same size as one wide head. Every head still sees every token; the gain is that heads can learn different relations.

mcq.q: Why does RoPE make the query-key score depend on relative position?
o: It adds a learned vector for each position to the embeddings at the input
It rotates the value vectors so the output encodes distance
It masks every token outside a fixed window around the query
It adds sine and cosine waves to the token embeddings once, before layer 1
Rotating q by angle mθ and k by nθ leaves their dot product a function of m minus n
mcq.why: A rotation preserves lengths, and the dot product of two rotated vectors depends on the difference of their angles. Learned absolute vectors and sinusoids added at the input are the older schemes.

mcq.q: A decoder has d_model = 4096 and 32 layers. Roughly how many parameters are in its blocks, embeddings excluded?
o: About 0.5B
About 6.4B
About 1.6B
About 25.8B
About 64B
mcq.why: 12 × 32 × 4096² is about 6.44B: 4 d² per layer for the Q, K, V and output projections and 8 d² for a 4x feed-forward. That is the scale of a 7B model once embeddings are added.

open.q: Walk me through one block of a modern decoder like Llama, and tell me where the parameters live.
open.probe: Whether you know the whole layer and its modern variants, not only attention.
a: RMSNorm, then causal multi-head attention with RoPE applied to queries and keys, then add the input back
RMSNorm again, a per-token feed-forward network (SwiGLU in Llama) about 4 times wider, add back; the block repeats N times
Residuals keep gradients flowing through deep stacks; pre-norm trains stably without the warmup post-norm needed
Per layer, about 4 d² in attention and 8 d² in the feed-forward network, so the FFN holds about two thirds
Check: GPT-3, 96 layers at 12,288, gives about 174B by 12 × L × d², close to the published 175B

say: The way I'd draw it: normalise, attend, add the input back, then normalise, a feed-forward on each token, add back again, and that repeats N times.

Heads let it look for several things at once at the same cost. Position has to be put in because attention doesn't know order, and in Llama-style models that's RoPE, which rotates the queries and keys so the score depends on distance.
People are often surprised that about two thirds of the weights are in the feed-forward part, not in attention.
avoid: Saying RoPE extends to any length for free: past the training length it needs frequency scaling and usually some fine-tuning.

topics.title: Encoder, decoder, encoder-decoder
topics.brief: The mask and the training objective decide the shape. BERT is an encoder that sees both sides and is trained on masked tokens, so it understands but does not generate; GPT is a causal decoder trained on the next token, so it generates; T5 and BART read with an encoder and write with a decoder. The nuance: instruction-tuned decoders now classify by prompting, but for high-volume understanding a small encoder is still far cheaper and faster.
points: Masked LM (BERT): hide about 15% of tokens (of those, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token, 10% unchanged) and predict them from both sides, which gives strong bidirectional representations
Why BERT does not generate: it learned to fill blanks given both sides, never to predict the next token from the left alone, so it has no natural token-by-token procedure
Causal LM (GPT, Llama): predicts the next token under a causal mask; every position is a training example, and generation is the same step repeated

Encoder-decoder (T5, BART): the encoder reads the input bidirectionally, the decoder generates causally and cross-attends to it; T5 pretrains by replacing spans with sentinel tokens and generating the missing spans
Uses: encoders for classification, NER, embeddings and cross-encoder reranking; decoders for generation and most general LLMs; encoder-decoders for translation and summarization
In an assistant: a fine-tuned small encoder for intent or routing runs in milliseconds on modest hardware; a decoder LLM takes open requests, out-of-scope turns and changing labels
production: DistilBERT keeps about 97% of BERT's language-understanding performance with 40% fewer parameters and about 60% faster inference
A 2026 preprint found fine-tuned RoBERTa beat Claude Haiku on ATIS and tied on CLINC150, but the LLM caught far more out-of-scope queries, at about 981 ms against 2.4 ms p50
A common pattern: label data with an LLM, have people review it, then distil into a small encoder for serving

read.label: Jay Alammar: The Illustrated BERT, ELMo and co.
read.why: Masked LM and how BERT is used for classification.

read.label: Hugging Face LLM course: How do Transformers work?
read.why: Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder side by side.

read.label: Stanford SLP3: ch. 9 Masked Language Models
read.why: BERT and fine-tuning, properly.

mcq.q: You need intent classification at 2,000 requests per second, 80 stable intents, thousands of labelled examples. Which shape fits best?
o: A decoder LLM prompted zero-shot on every request
A decoder LLM with a long few-shot prompt per request
An encoder-decoder that generates the intent name as text
A small fine-tuned encoder such as DistilBERT with a softmax head
Mean-pooled vanilla BERT vectors compared to the intent names
mcq.why: Stable labels, plenty of data and tight volume and latency are exactly where a fine-tuned encoder wins on cost and speed. Vanilla mean-pooled BERT is poor for similarity, and generating labels with a decoder costs far more per call.

mcq.q: Why can't BERT generate fluent text the way GPT does?
o: Its vocabulary has no end-of-sequence token
It was trained to fill masked tokens from both sides, never to predict the next token from the left
It has no attention layers, only feed-forward ones
It is too small; a masked model at GPT-3 scale generates equally well
Its position embeddings cannot be extended past 512
mcq.why: Generation needs a left-to-right next-token model. BERT's objective and its lack of a causal mask give it no such procedure, whatever its size.

mcq.q: What does the causal mask let a decoder do during training?
o: Ignore padding tokens when sequences in a batch differ in length
Attend to the encoder's output while generating
Hide about 15% of tokens and predict them from both sides
Skip the softmax at masked positions to save compute
Train on one sequence as many next-token predictions in one pass, without seeing the future
mcq.why: Blocking attention to later positions means every position predicts its next token at once. Ignoring pad tokens is the padding mask, a different mask.

open.q: We have a BERT-based intent classifier in production. A colleague wants to replace it with a GPT-style LLM. How do you think about it?
open.probe: Whether you can tie the architecture to cost, latency and the failure you care about.
a: BERT is an encoder: bidirectional, masked-token training, strong representations; GPT is a causal decoder that generates
The encoder wins on volume, latency, cost and determinism for a stable closed label set with data
The LLM wins on scarce data, changing labels, out-of-scope and turns that need reasoning
So often both: the encoder takes the confident bulk, the LLM the uncertain slice, measured on per-intent recall and out-of-scope false accepts
The LLM can also label new data that is then distilled into the encoder

say: I wouldn't swap it outright. BERT reads both directions and was trained to fill in blanks, so it's great at understanding and it's cheap.
GPT was trained to predict the next word, so it generates, and it copes better with new phrasing and things we don't support.
The way I'd do it is keep the encoder for the confident traffic and send the uncertain slice to the LLM, then measure both on the same held-out set.
avoid: Calling encoders obsolete: they are still the cheap default for classification, embeddings and reranking.

topics.title: The cost of attention, the KV cache and FlashAttention
topics.brief: Full attention scores every token against every other, so compute grows with the square of the length. In generation the keys and values of past tokens never change, so they are cached and each new token computes only its own; the cache then becomes the memory bottleneck. The nuance: FlashAttention makes attention exact and memory-efficient but does not remove the quadratic compute, and grouped-query attention is what shrinks the cache.
points: O(n²): the score matrix is n by n per head per layer, so doubling the context roughly quadruples attention compute

FlashAttention: computes exact attention in tiles held in fast on-chip SRAM with an online softmax, never writing the n by n matrix to GPU memory; memory becomes linear in n and it runs faster by cutting memory reads and writes, but the FLOPs stay quadratic
KV cache: under the causal mask, earlier tokens' keys and values are fixed, so they are stored per layer; each new token computes its own Q, K and V and attends over the cache

Size per token: 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes; Llama 2 7B (32 layers, 32 heads of 128, fp16) is 2 × 32 × 4096 × 2 = 524,288 bytes, about 0.5 MB, so about 2 GB for 4,000 tokens of one sequence
MQA and GQA: multi-query attention shares one K and V head across all query heads; grouped-query shares one per group; Llama 3 8B has 8 KV heads for 32 query heads, a quarter of the cache

Prefill against decode: prefill processes the prompt in parallel and is compute-bound; decode emits one token at a time, rereading the weights and the cache, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound, which is why cache size and batching decide serving cost
production: vLLM's PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual memory pages, which cuts fragmentation so more sequences fit on one GPU
Prefix caching reuses the cache of a shared system prompt across requests; providers price cached input tokens lower
Quantising the cache from fp16 to 8 bits halves its memory, at a small quality cost to be measured
Track time to first token (prefill) and per-token latency (decode) separately; they have different fixes

read.label: Lilian Weng: Large Transformer model inference optimization
read.why: The KV cache cost and the main inference levers.

read.label: Ainslie et al.: GQA, grouped-query attention
read.why: Sharing keys and values across heads to shrink the cache.

mcq.q: Llama 2 7B (32 layers, hidden 4096, fp16, no GQA) serves 8 concurrent sequences of 4,000 tokens. Roughly how much memory does the KV cache take?
o: About 2 GB
About 0.5 GB
About 16 GB
About 64 GB
About 128 MB
mcq.why: About 0.5 MB per token (2 × 32 × 4096 × 2 bytes) × 4,000 tokens × 8 sequences is about 16.8 GB. 2 GB is one sequence.

mcq.q: What does FlashAttention change?
o: It approximates attention with a low-rank projection so compute becomes linear
It shares keys and values across heads to shrink memory
It restricts each token to a fixed window of neighbours
It caches keys and values between decoding steps
It computes exact attention in on-chip tiles without storing the n by n matrix, so memory traffic drops while compute stays quadratic
mcq.why: FlashAttention is exact and IO-aware: it avoids materialising the score matrix in GPU memory. Low-rank and windowed attention are approximations; sharing K and V is GQA; caching is the KV cache.

mcq.q: A model moves from 32 KV heads to 8 (grouped-query attention). What mainly changes?
o: The KV cache and decode memory traffic drop to about a quarter, with small quality loss
Attention compute becomes linear in sequence length
Prefill becomes memory-bound instead of compute-bound
The number of query heads drops to 8
Its outputs become identical to FlashAttention's
mcq.why: Query heads stay at 32; groups of 4 share one K and V head, so the cache is a quarter of the size. The quadratic score computation is unchanged.

open.q: Our assistant's latency and GPU bill jump when conversations get long. Explain why, from the mechanism.
open.probe: Whether you can connect attention's cost and the KV cache to a real serving symptom.
a: Each new token attends over every earlier one, so per-token decode work and the KV cache grow with the conversation
The cache is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per token, about 0.5 MB a token for a 7B model without GQA, so long chats limit how many sequences fit in a batch
Decode is memory-bound, so fewer concurrent sequences means a higher cost per token
Levers: trim or summarise history, prefix caching for the shared system prompt, GQA models, a quantised cache, paged cache management
Measure time to first token and per-token latency separately, since prefill and decode have different fixes

say: I'd explain it from the KV cache. Every new token looks back at all the earlier ones, so the cache grows with the conversation, about half a megabyte a token on a 7B model without grouped-query attention.
That eats the GPU memory you'd use for batching, and decode is limited by memory traffic, so the cost per token goes up.
The fixes I'd look at are trimming or summarising history, caching the shared system prompt, and models with grouped-query attention.
avoid: Saying FlashAttention makes attention linear: memory becomes linear, compute stays quadratic.

topics.title: Tokenization: BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece
topics.brief: Models read subword tokens from a fixed vocabulary, roughly 30k to 200k pieces, that can compose any word. BPE learns merges by frequency, WordPiece picks merges by a likelihood score, and SentencePiece is a library that trains BPE or unigram models on raw text with spaces as symbols. The nuance: tokenization explains cost, context use and odd failures on spelling, digits and IDs.
points: Why subwords: a word vocabulary explodes and cannot represent unseen words; characters make sequences long, and attention cost grows with length

BPE (Sennrich et al., 2016): start from characters or bytes, merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, repeat until the vocabulary reaches its target size; encoding replays the learned merges in the order they were learned
Byte-level BPE (GPT-2, RoBERTa): the 256 byte values are the base, so any string can be encoded and nothing is out of vocabulary; GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257

WordPiece (BERT): merges the pair with the best likelihood score (in the Hugging Face description, pair count divided by the product of the part counts), marks continuations with '##', and at inference takes the longest matching piece from the left

SentencePiece and unigram: SentencePiece reads raw text with the space as a visible symbol (▁), so no language-specific pre-tokenizer; its unigram option starts large and prunes the pieces whose removal least hurts likelihood; T5 and Llama 1 and 2 use SentencePiece

Consequences: cost and context are counted in tokens; other languages and digits often take more tokens; letters inside a token are invisible, so spelling backwards or counting letters is hard; account numbers split unpredictably
production: Pricing and context limits are in tokens, and the same text can take noticeably more tokens outside English
Llama 3 moved to a 128K-token BPE vocabulary (built on tiktoken) from Llama 2's 32K SentencePiece one, so the same text takes fewer tokens
In an assistant, account numbers, amounts and dates are extracted by a schema-validated tool call or code and checked in code, because the model sees them as token fragments

read.label: Hugging Face LLM course: Byte-pair encoding tokenization
read.why: BPE worked step by step, with code.

read.label: Stanford SLP3: ch. 2 Words and Tokens
read.why: The BPE section only.

mcq.q: BPE training has counted all adjacent pairs. Which pair does it merge next?
o: The pair whose merge most raises training likelihood relative to its parts
The longest substring already present in the vocabulary
The most frequent adjacent pair of current symbols in the corpus
The piece whose removal least lowers likelihood
A random pair, weighted by frequency, so tokenization varies
mcq.why: BPE is greedy on frequency. Choosing by likelihood relative to the parts is WordPiece; pruning by likelihood is the unigram model.

mcq.q: A tokenizer turns 'playing' into 'play' and '##ing'. What is it?
o: Byte-level BPE, which marks spaces with a special byte symbol
SentencePiece, which marks word starts with ▁
A character-level tokenizer with a suffix list
A unigram model that sampled one of several segmentations
WordPiece, which marks word-internal pieces with '##'
mcq.why: '##' marks a continuation piece in BERT's WordPiece. SentencePiece marks the start of a word instead, and byte-level BPE in GPT-2 folds the space into the next token.

mcq.q: Why does a byte-level BPE model never produce an unknown token?
o: Its base vocabulary is all 256 byte values, so any string can fall back to bytes
Its vocabulary of over 50,000 pieces covers every word in common languages
Unknown words are mapped to the nearest known word by embedding similarity
It lowercases and strips accents before encoding
It switches to characters at inference whenever a word is rare
mcq.why: Every UTF-8 string is a sequence of bytes, and every byte is in the vocabulary. Rare words cost more tokens, but they never become [UNK].

open.q: Why do models use subword tokens, and what does that mean for a banking assistant in practice?
open.probe: Whether you understand BPE and can connect tokenization to cost and to failures on IDs and numbers.
a: Words: the vocabulary explodes and unseen words break; characters: sequences get long; subwords: a fixed vocabulary that composes anything
BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pair again and again, and encoding replays the merges; byte-level means no unknown tokens
WordPiece merges by a likelihood score and uses '##'; SentencePiece handles raw text with the space as a symbol
Practice: cost and context are tokens; account numbers and amounts split into fragments, so extract and validate them in code rather than trusting the model's reading

say: Subwords sit in the middle. Whole words blow up the vocabulary and break on new words, and characters make everything too long.
BPE starts from bytes and keeps merging the most common pair, so common words end up as one token and rare ones as a few pieces.
In a banking assistant that matters because an account number is a handful of odd fragments to the model, so I'd pull those out and check them in code.
avoid: Saying WordPiece is BPE with likelihood as if they were the same: related, but with different merge rules and a different inference procedure.

topics.title: Decoding: greedy, beam, temperature, top-k, top-p
topics.brief: The model outputs a probability distribution over the next token; decoding decides which token to take. Temperature reshapes the distribution, top-k and top-p cut its tail, and greedy and beam search are deterministic searches. The nuance: for anything the assistant acts on, use temperature 0 or schema-constrained decoding, and know that even temperature 0 is not guaranteed byte-identical across runs.
points: Greedy and beam: greedy takes the most likely token each step; beam search keeps the b best partial sequences; good for translation and summarization, bland and repetitive on open text (Holtzman et al., 2019)
Temperature: divides the logits by T before the softmax; below 1 sharpens, above 1 flattens, toward 0 it approaches greedy; it never changes the ranking of tokens
Top-k: samples from the k most likely tokens; a fixed k is too wide when the model is confident and too narrow when it is not
Top-p (nucleus): samples from the smallest set whose probabilities add up to at least p, so the set shrinks when the distribution is peaked and grows when it is flat
Constrained decoding: a grammar or JSON schema masks invalid tokens at each step, so the output always parses; the values still need checking in code
Temperature 0 is not a determinism guarantee: batching, floating-point order and provider updates can change outputs; pin model versions and log outputs
production: Classification, extraction and tool arguments: temperature 0 or structured outputs against a JSON schema, then validation and one retry with the error message
Open replies: a moderate temperature with top-p is a common starting point, tuned on an evaluation set rather than by feel
Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths at a moderate temperature and take the majority answer, trading cost for accuracy

read.label: Holtzman et al.: The curious case of neural text degeneration
read.why: Why greedy and beam go bland, and how nucleus sampling fixes it.

mcq.q: The next-token distribution is very peaked: one token has probability 0.97. With top-p = 0.9, what can be sampled?
o: The top 90% of the vocabulary by probability
Only that token, because it alone reaches 0.9
Any token with probability above 0.1
The 40 most likely tokens, rescaled
That token and the next most likely one, for variety
mcq.why: The nucleus is the smallest set whose probability reaches p. One token at 0.97 already exceeds 0.9, so the set has one member.

mcq.q: Why does top-p adapt better than top-k?
o: It always samples from more tokens, which adds variety
It changes the ranking of tokens before sampling
It is deterministic, so outputs repeat exactly
Its candidate set grows or shrinks with how flat the distribution is, while k stays fixed
It learns a temperature for each prompt
mcq.why: A fixed k includes junk when the model is confident and cuts good options when it is unsure. Top-p sizes the set by probability mass instead.

mcq.q: An assistant extracts transfer amounts from customer messages. Which decoding setup fits?
o: Temperature 1 with top-p 0.95, to cover more phrasings
A large beam, to find the best overall parse
Temperature 0, which guarantees identical output on every call
Top-k of 1 at temperature 1.5, for confident but varied output
Temperature 0 or a schema-constrained output, with the amount validated in code
mcq.why: Anything acted on should be as deterministic and well-formed as possible, and then checked in code. Temperature 0 is near-deterministic but not guaranteed identical, so it cannot replace validation.

open.q: How would you set decoding for an intent classifier, an entity extractor and the assistant's open replies?
open.probe: Whether you match the knob to the task and know its limits.
a: Classifier and extractor: temperature 0 or constrained decoding to an enum or schema; validate in code and retry once with the error
Open replies: some temperature with top-p, tuned on an evaluation set for tone and accuracy
Temperature reshapes the distribution; top-k and top-p truncate it, and top-p adapts to the model's confidence
Temperature 0 is near-deterministic, not guaranteed; pin model versions and log outputs

say: For anything the assistant acts on, like an intent or an amount, I'd use temperature zero or constrain the output to a schema, then check the values in code.
For the open replies I'd allow a bit of temperature with top-p, and tune it on an eval set.
I wouldn't promise byte-identical output even at zero, because batching and model updates can still change it. That's pretty much why the checks live in code.
avoid: Claiming lower temperature fixes hallucination: it adds no knowledge.

topics.title: From pretrained model to assistant
topics.brief: Pretraining on next-token prediction gives a model that continues text. Supervised fine-tuning on instruction and response pairs teaches format and behaviour, and preference tuning (RLHF or DPO) makes it prefer the answers people rank higher. The nuance: post-training shapes behaviour far more than knowledge, and fine-tuning on facts the model does not know can teach it to guess.
points: Pretraining and scaling: next-token loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute (Kaplan et al., 2020); Chinchilla (2022) found compute-optimal training uses about 20 tokens per parameter, and labs now train smaller models on far more tokens because inference cost matters
SFT: supervised fine-tuning on (instruction, response) pairs teaches format, instruction following and tone, and little new knowledge

RLHF: people rank responses, a reward model learns the ranking, then PPO optimises the policy against it with a KL penalty that keeps it near the SFT model; InstructGPT's 1.3B RLHF model was preferred by labellers over 175B GPT-3

DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): no reward model and no RL loop; a classification-style loss raises the log-probability ratio of the preferred answer over the rejected one, relative to a frozen reference model, with β setting how far it may drift
In-context learning: adapting from examples in the prompt with no weight update; sensitive to example choice, order and format; retrieved similar examples usually beat fixed ones
The hallucination link: fine-tuning on facts the model does not already know teaches confident guessing (covered in Lilian Weng's survey), so knowledge belongs in retrieval and behaviour in tuning
production: Llama 2-Chat: SFT, then RLHF with rejection-sampling fine-tuning and PPO
DPO and its variants are widely used in open-model post-training because they are simpler and more stable than PPO
Reasoning models add RL with verifiable rewards (checkable maths answers, passing code tests), for example GRPO in DeepSeek's work

read.label: Stanford SLP3: ch. 8 Post-training
read.why: Instruction tuning and preference tuning, clearly.

read.label: Ouyang et al.: InstructGPT
read.why: SFT, a reward model and PPO, with the 1.3B result.

read.label: Rafailov et al.: Direct preference optimization
read.why: The abstract and the loss.

mcq.q: A team fine-tunes on 5,000 Q&A pairs of internal facts the base model never saw, and hallucination goes up. Most likely why?
o: The learning rate was too low for the facts to be stored
Training it to state facts it does not know teaches it to answer confidently without knowledge
SFT cannot change model outputs, only formatting
5,000 pairs is too few; 50,000 would have fixed it
The tokenizer could not represent the new terms
mcq.why: The model learns the behaviour 'give a confident answer' without the knowledge behind it, which is guessing. Facts that change belong in retrieval.

mcq.q: What does DPO remove compared with RLHF using PPO?
o: The human preference data; it learns preferences from raw text
The reference model; it needs only the policy being trained
The SFT stage; it starts from the pretrained model
The separate reward model and the RL sampling loop
Any limit on drift; the policy may move freely
mcq.why: DPO trains directly on preferred and rejected pairs with a loss relative to a frozen reference model. It still uses preference data, usually starts from an SFT model, and β plays the role of the KL constraint.

mcq.q: In RLHF, what is the KL penalty for?
o: Keeping the policy near the SFT model so it does not exploit the reward model with odd outputs
Making the reward model's scores calibrated probabilities
Smoothing PPO's gradients so it converges faster
Forcing the policy to match the pretraining data token by token
Penalising answers longer than the SFT model's average
mcq.why: A reward model is an imperfect proxy. Without the penalty, the policy finds outputs that score high but read badly; the KL term keeps it close to the SFT distribution.

open.q: How does a pretrained model become a helpful assistant, and where would you plug in your own changes for a bank?
open.probe: Whether you know each stage, what it changes, and which lever fits a bank's needs.
a: Pretraining on next-token prediction gives a text continuer with broad knowledge
SFT on instruction and response pairs teaches format and behaviour
Preference tuning: RLHF (a reward model, then PPO with a KL penalty) or DPO (a direct loss on preferred against rejected pairs, relative to a frozen reference)
Own changes: prompts and retrieval first for policy and product knowledge; tuning (often LoRA SFT, maybe DPO on reviewed pairs) for tone, format and refusals
Never tune in facts that change: they go stale and can raise guessing

say: Pretraining gives you something that continues text. Then supervised fine-tuning on instruction and answer pairs teaches it to follow instructions, and preference tuning, RLHF or now often DPO, teaches it which answers people prefer.
For a bank I'd keep the facts in retrieval and use tuning only for behaviour, like format and when to refuse.
Tuning facts in goes stale, and it can make the model guess.
avoid: Saying SFT teaches the model your company's knowledge: it mostly teaches behaviour.

topics.title: Prompt, RAG, fine-tune or LoRA
topics.brief: Start with prompting; add retrieval when the gap is knowledge that is private, large or changing; fine-tune when the gap is behaviour, format, tone, or cost and latency at scale; LoRA makes that fine-tune cheap. The nuance: the levers combine, and hallucination is reduced by grounding and checks, not by a lower temperature or by tuning facts in.
points: Prompting: no training and fast to change; limited by context length, consistency, and the per-call cost of long prompts
RAG: retrieve relevant passages at query time and condition on them; updatable without retraining, citable, and the main lever against hallucination on facts; capped by retrieval quality
Fine-tuning: changes weights for behaviour, format, tone or a narrow skill, or lets a smaller model match a larger one on one task

LoRA (Hu et al., 2021): freeze W and learn ΔW = BA with rank r far below d; up to 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and about 3 times less GPU memory than full GPT-3 175B fine-tuning, no added latency once BA is merged, and adapters can be swapped per task; QLoRA trains the adapters on a 4-bit quantised frozen base

Reducing hallucination: ground in retrieved evidence with citations, constrain the answer to that context, use tools for facts and arithmetic, allow abstention, and measure faithfulness on a regression set
Classifier pattern: label with an LLM, have people review, distil into a small encoder
production: Bank knowledge (fees, policies, product terms) changes and needs citations, so it lives in retrieval over versioned documents; tone and refusal style live in prompts or a light tune
Multi-LoRA serving: one base model with many small adapters chosen per request (vLLM and LoRAX support this)
QLoRA fine-tuned a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU by keeping the frozen base in 4-bit

read.label: Hu et al.: LoRA, low-rank adaptation of large language models
read.why: The abstract and the method section.

read.label: Lilian Weng: Extrinsic hallucinations in LLMs
read.why: Causes and mitigation, including why tuning new facts hurts.

mcq.q: A fee schedule changes every quarter and answers must cite the current document. What fits best?
o: Fine-tune on the fee schedule each quarter so the model knows it
Train a new LoRA adapter each quarter and swap it in at release
Retrieval over the versioned documents, with citations in the answer
Lower the temperature so the model states fees more precisely
A system prompt with every fee table, so no retrieval is needed
mcq.why: Changing knowledge that must be cited is the textbook case for retrieval: update the documents, not the weights. Tuning facts in goes stale and cannot cite.

mcq.q: Why does a merged LoRA adapter add no inference latency?
o: The adapters run on a separate GPU in parallel with the base
LoRA prunes the base weights, so the model gets smaller
The base is stored in 4-bit during inference
Only the attention layers run; the feed-forward layers are skipped
BA has the same shape as W, so it is added into W once and the model runs as before
mcq.why: W' = W + BA is an ordinary weight matrix of the original shape. Keeping the base in 4-bit is QLoRA, a training memory trick, not the reason.

mcq.q: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?
o: The adapters are quantised to 4 bits after training to speed up inference
The rank is chosen automatically for each layer
The base weights are also updated, at low precision
The frozen base is stored in 4-bit so large models fit for fine-tuning on one GPU
Documents are stored in adapters, which replaces retrieval
mcq.why: QLoRA quantises the frozen base to 4-bit and backpropagates through it into higher-precision adapters, which is why a 65B model fit on one 48 GB GPU.

open.q: Our assistant should answer questions about fund fees and account rules in a consistent, careful tone. Prompt, RAG, fine-tune or LoRA?
open.probe: Whether you separate knowledge from behaviour and know what each lever costs.
a: Prompt first: instructions, examples and an output schema, measured on an evaluation set
Fees and rules are knowledge that changes and needs citations, so RAG over versioned documents, with abstention when evidence is weak
Tone and format: prompt first; if still inconsistent at volume, a LoRA fine-tune on reviewed examples
Do not tune facts in: they go stale and raise guessing
Measure faithfulness and citation accuracy on a regression set before and after each change

say: My rule is knowledge goes in retrieval, behaviour goes in tuning, and I try prompting before either.
Fees and account rules change and need a citation, so that's RAG over the current documents. If the tone still drifts at volume, I'd do a LoRA fine-tune, because it's cheap and you can swap adapters.
At alfred_ we went a step further for one case: the model only sees opaque handles for real items, and code reattaches the real ids, so the ids it acts on come from code, not from the model.
avoid: Saying lower temperature fixes hallucination: it adds no knowledge.
Claiming the handle scheme makes hallucination impossible: it removes one kind of invented id, and checks still run.

modules.title: You: your story and your work
modules.blurb: Your intro, why this role, and your work told as it is in the code today. Explain each aloud, then compare.

topics.title: Tell me about yourself
topics.brief: Research, shipping, production assistants, and the layer in front of the agent: understanding and improving it from real conversations.
points: They may ask: What does alfred_ do?
They may ask: What do you own there?
They may ask: Have you worked on a chatbot or virtual assistant?
They may ask: Which NLU platforms have you used?
production: If they ask what alfred_ is, in a line: An AI executive assistant that works over text message and the web. It handles people's email and calendar end to end, for 5,000-plus active users.

If they ask which NLU platforms you've used: Honestly, not Dialogflow or Lex in production. I've built the layer in front of LLM agents myself: routing, entity resolution, confirmation in code. The understanding there is an LLM with typed tool schemas, not a trained classifier, but the modelling and the error analysis are the same work, and I'd pick up the platform quickly.

open.q: Tell me about yourself
open.probe: The opener. Land on conversational AI and the NLP under it.
a: Sure. I started out in computer science research at UIC, where I worked on applied ML and LLM systems. That gave me a pretty strong foundation in actually building and evaluating these systems, rather than just using the models.

From there I joined WheelPrice, which was a much more startup-oriented environment. I was working across the stack and got a lot more exposure to shipping things that were actually being used by customers. It was a small engineering team, so I had to be pretty broad — backend, AI, infrastructure, and product work all kind of blended together.

After that I joined alfred_, where I've been working as a founding LLM engineer. It's an AI assistant, and my work has become much more focused on reliability and evaluation — things like building the eval harness, production failure detection, working memory, and making sure agent changes actually improve the product rather than just looking better on a benchmark.

The common thread through all of that has really been building AI systems in environments where you don't have a perfectly defined problem in front of you. You have to figure out what's broken, decide what to build, and then own it through production.

And the closest part to this role is what sits in front of the agent. At alfred_ a fast first pass decides whether a message can be answered or needs the heavier agent, things like 'that email' resolve to real records, anything that sends goes through a confirm step in code, and a scanner reads real conversations every day to find what went wrong. So building an assistant and improving it from its transcripts is pretty much the work I already do.

avoid: Never say you've used Dialogflow, Lex, CLU, Rasa, Kore.ai or Cognigy.
Never mention alfred_'s funding, a crunch, or colleagues' names.

topics.title: Why this role?
topics.brief: Vanguard is doing generative AI in the right order, and keeping an assistant inside its lines is my daily work.
points: They may ask: Why Vanguard?
They may ask: What do you know about our assistants?
They may ask: Why classic NLU when everyone is moving to LLMs?
production: If they ask why classic NLU at all: I think the classic layer is the part you can measure and control: a confusion matrix, a threshold, a test set. The LLM is great for the long tail and out-of-scope. Most good assistants I've read about use both, and that's how alfred_ works too.

If they ask what you know about the scale: From what I read, your chat already serves more than 2 million investors a month, and you're adding AI features to it. At that volume a small error rate is a lot of people, so the evaluation has to come first.

open.q: Why this role?
open.probe: After the intro, or when they ask why Vanguard or why conversational AI.
a: Honestly, it's the way Vanguard is doing it. From what I read, the generative AI went to crew first, Crew Assist and agent assist in the contact center, and the client-facing side is staged: summaries for advisers in beta, then a pilot inside Digital Advisor. I think that's the right order, and it's how I'd do it.

And the concern your CIO named, keeping the bot from veering into advice and watching for hallucinations, is pretty much the problem I work on. At alfred_ anything that sends or deletes goes through a confirm step in code before it runs, and a scanner reads real conversations every day to find what went wrong.

The two areas in the role are the two halves of what I do. One is the assistant: how the conversation is designed, how intents and entities are modelled, and how you find and fix what's going wrong in production. The other is the NLP underneath: classification, embeddings, how the models work.
So it's the work I already do, in a place where being right matters more than being first.

topics.title: What have you built that's closest to this?
topics.brief: A first pass that answers or escalates, entity resolution in chat, a confirm flow in code and a failure scanner in production; stages driven by tools in voice; TF-IDF weighted embeddings in research.
points: They may ask: How does the first pass decide to escalate?
They may ask: How do you decide when to ask the user?
They may ask: How do you find failures?
They may ask: Was any of it on a platform like Dialogflow?
production: If they ask about WheelPrice: At WheelPrice I built an AI fitment assistant that could only answer through tools against verified data.

If they ask about a classic platform: Not in production. The concepts map closely: a page with a form in Dialogflow CX is a stage with required slots, and a route is a transition. I'd want a week with their taxonomy and their transcripts.
If they ask about voice: I own alfred_'s voice agent, phone and web. In MockFlow-AI the pipeline was Deepgram Nova-2 for speech and Silero for voice activity.

open.q: What have you built that's closest to this?
open.probe: When they ask about your experience with chatbots, virtual assistants or NLU. Outcome first, one design choice, then stop.
a: The closest is alfred_. It's an AI assistant over text and the web. A fast first pass answers what it can from what it can read and escalates the rest to a heavier agent, and code guards turn a reply that promises an action into an escalation instead of shipping it. I also built entity resolution in chat, so 'the second email' or 'that meeting' points at a real record, and the confirm flow: anything that sends gets a preview first and runs only on an explicit confirm, with floors in code that no prompt can override.

Then error analysis. I built a production failure scanner that reads real conversations, separates genuine failures from expected behaviour, and promotes the real bugs for triage. Those feed a replay bench of real production turns, graded by a person, so a change is judged on what users actually hit before it ships.

Before that, MockFlow-AI: a real-time voice interview platform I built from scratch, under 400 milliseconds end to end. The conversation moves through stages in a state machine, and the model can only move it by calling a transition tool. That's the nearest thing I've built to flows and pages.
And on the NLP side, MetaRAG at UIC: TF-IDF weighted embeddings with recursive chunking got 82.5% precision against a 73.3% baseline, and 0.925 Hit Rate at 10.

avoid: Don't call alfred_'s classifier 'Dialogflow-like' or name a platform you haven't used.

topics.title: How your background fits, and the gaps
topics.brief: Most of the role maps onto work you've done; the classic NLU platforms and a trained intent classifier are new, and you say so first.
points: Done: a first pass that answers or escalates; entity resolution in chat; a confirm flow with floors in code; grounding guards; a failure scanner over real conversations.
Also done: a voice state machine in MockFlow-AI; TF-IDF weighted embeddings in MetaRAG; a from-scratch Transformer.
Not done: Dialogflow CX, Lex, CLU, Rasa, Kore.ai or Cognigy in production.
Not done: a trained intent classifier or NER model in production; an intent taxonomy in the hundreds; contact-centre analytics at enterprise volume.

open.q: How does your background fit this role?
open.probe: Is it real, and are you honest about the gaps?
a: Most of it maps directly. The role is building and improving assistants: conversation design, intents and entities, error analysis, production improvements, on strong NLP.

At alfred_ I built the parts that do that work: the first pass that decides whether a turn can be answered or needs the heavier agent, entity resolution in chat so 'that email' points at a real record, the confirm flow and code floors on anything that sends, and the scanner that finds failures in real conversations.

What I haven't done is ship on a classic NLU platform, or train an intent classifier for a taxonomy of hundreds of intents. In alfred_ the understanding is an LLM with typed tool schemas, checked in code. The error analysis and the design underneath are the same work; the platform is new.

avoid: Don't say alfred_ has a trained intent classifier, a decision layer or a risk score.

topics.title: What your assistant may do on its own
topics.brief: Anything that changes the world goes through a preview, then an explicit confirm, with floors in code that no prompt can override and idempotency on retries.
points: Preview first: the first call to a sending tool returns a preview and stashes the arguments as a pending confirmation.
Explicit confirm: only a second call with a real confirmation executes; sends need that prior preview.
Code floors: destructive actions and external sends always confirm; a bare 'yes' can't approve several pending sends; large sweeps hit a scale threshold.
Idempotency: a retried send replays the first result instead of sending again.

open.q: How does your assistant decide what it can do without asking?
open.probe: Whether safety is a rule you can test or a prompt you hope holds.
a: Anything that changes the world goes through a two-step confirm. The first call to a tool like send email returns a preview, not an action, and the arguments are kept as a pending confirmation. Only a second call with an explicit confirmation executes it.

On top of that there are floors in code that no prompt can override: destructive actions and external sends always confirm, and a bare 'yes' can't approve several sends at once. Retries go through idempotency keys, so a double send replays the first result.
I think that's the right split: the model is good at understanding what someone meant; whether it's safe to send an email on their behalf should be a rule you can test.

avoid: Talk only about what's live: the confirm flow, the floors and idempotency. No verdicts, no risk score.

topics.title: How your assistant knows what 'that email' means
topics.brief: You built entity management in chat: everything in play is a typed entity with a real id and a lifetime, kept outside the model, so references resolve to records rather than guesses.
points: Typed entities: email, thread, draft, event, task, contact and more, each with its real id.
Lifetimes: short for drafts and emails, longer for events and tasks; an event expires after it happens.
Resolution: the prompt lists them numbered with references; the tool receives a real id.
Matching: contacts and events are resolved by deterministic matching with thresholds; when two candidates are too close, it asks.
Honest limit: 'the second one' is resolved by the model reading the numbered list, not by code.

open.q: A user says 'reply to the second one'. How does your assistant know what that means?
open.probe: Dialogue state and entity resolution, and honesty about where the model still decides.
a: Everything in play in a conversation, an email, a thread, an event, a task, a contact, is kept as a typed entity outside the model, with its real id and a lifetime.
The prompt shows them as a numbered list with references, so when someone says 'the second one', the model resolves it against that list and the tool gets a real id, not a guess.
Contacts and events are resolved by deterministic matching: several sources merged, a similarity threshold, and if two candidates are too close it asks rather than picks.
Honestly, the ordinal itself is the model reading the list; if I were hardening it, I'd move that into code too.

topics.title: How your assistant stops claiming what it didn't do
topics.brief: Claims of actions and searches are checked in code against the turn's tool-execution ledger; a model-based verifier is a narrow, flagged backstop, not the main check.
points: Ledger check: a reply that claims an action, a search or a saved item is checked against what the tools actually did that turn.
First-pass guards: a reply that promises an action or claims it's done becomes an escalation instead of shipping.
Strict-ID memory: the model sees opaque handles; code drops any it didn't issue and reattaches the real ids.
Limit: the model still writes the wording, so this removes invented threads and owners, not every wrong sentence.

open.q: How do you stop your assistant claiming things it didn't do?
open.probe: Grounding you built, and whether you overclaim it.
a: We found the assistant sometimes claimed an action or a live fact with no tool behind it. So every reply that claims an action, a search or a saved item is checked against that turn's tool-execution ledger, in code, not by another model.
In the fast first pass, a reply that promises an action or says it's done is turned into an escalation instead of shipping.

For memory, the model only ever sees opaque handles, and code drops any handle it didn't issue, so it can't point at a thread that doesn't exist. It still writes the sentence, so I wouldn't call it hallucination-proof.
The lesson for me: the cheap deterministic check carries most of the weight; a model-based check is a narrow backstop.

avoid: Don't say an LLM verifier checks every reply, or that strict-ID makes hallucination impossible.

topics.title: The production failure scanner and the replay bench
topics.brief: Deterministic signals find candidate failures in real conversations, a model labels each, and only real agent bugs above a confidence bar are promoted; a replay bench judges changes on real turns, graded by a person.
points: Scan: deterministic signals and detectors over real conversations.
Classify: a model labels each candidate as an agent bug, a UX problem, a provider error or expected behaviour.
Promote: only agent bugs above a confidence bar; signals like a user dropping off never auto-promote.
Precision: joining against the tool-execution record killed false 'agent did nothing' flags.
Bench: real production turns replayed against a change, graded by a person; not run in CI.

open.q: Tell me about the production failure scanner.
open.probe: Error analysis you've actually run.
a: It scans real production conversations with deterministic signals and detectors, then a model classifies each candidate: an agent bug, a UX problem, a provider error, or expected behaviour.
Only real agent bugs above a confidence bar are promoted automatically, and some signals, like a user dropping off, never are, because they're too often not a failure.
The hard part is that second step: a lot of what looks like failure is the assistant correctly declining. Joining against the tool-execution record killed a lot of false flags.
The failures feed a replay bench of real turns, graded by a person, so a change is judged on what users actually hit. It's the transcript-review loop this role describes, automated.

avoid: Don't say evals run in CI.

topics.title: MetaRAG, your retrieval research
topics.brief: A retrieval framework for enterprise knowledge at UIC, accepted at IEEE CAI 2026: recursive chunking with TF-IDF weighted embeddings. Not alfred_ work.
points: Result: 82.5% precision against a 73.3% baseline, 0.925 Hit Rate at 10.
Production: about 10K queries a day, p99 under 300 ms, 25% hallucination reduction.
Lesson: get retrieval right before touching generation; sparse signals help dense embeddings on domain vocabulary.
Check before the call: how the TF-IDF weights enter the embedding, and how hallucination was measured.

open.q: Tell me about MetaRAG.
open.probe: Your NLP research, with its numbers.
a: MetaRAG was a retrieval framework for enterprise knowledge at UIC, accepted at IEEE CAI 2026. Recursive chunking with TF-IDF weighted embeddings got 82.5% precision against a 73.3% baseline, and 0.925 Hit Rate at 10.
It ran in a production code-translation use case at about 10K queries a day with p99 latency under 300 milliseconds, and it reduced hallucination by 25%.
The lesson that carries over to an assistant: get retrieval right before touching generation, and let sparse signals like TF-IDF help dense embeddings on domain vocabulary.

avoid: Don't improvise the weighting mechanism or the hallucination measure.

topics.title: Getting productive on their platform
topics.brief: The platform is what you'd learn; the work underneath you've done. Learn it on real work: taxonomy, transcripts, one small measurable fix end to end.
points: Week one: read the taxonomy and the confusion matrix, sit with real transcripts.
Map the pieces: a page with a form is a state with required slots; a route is a transition; an event handler is the no-match ladder.
Then one small fix end to end through their test cases and release process.

open.q: You haven't used our platform. How would you get productive?
open.probe: Honesty plus a credible plan.
a: Honestly, the platform is the part I'd learn; the work underneath it I've done. In the first week I'd read the intent taxonomy and the confusion matrix, sit with a few hundred real transcripts, and map the platform's pieces onto what I know.
Then I'd pick one small, measurable problem, a pair of confused intents or a page with a high no-match rate, and fix it end to end through the platform's test cases and release process.
That's how I work with any new stack: I built MockFlow-AI on LiveKit from scratch, and it runs under 400 milliseconds end to end.
